item.content:encoded:
Washington DC nonprofit The National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sued the government last year over the White House ballroom extension, has announced a $10 million fundraising campaign for legal defence in support of US landmark preservation.

National Trust for Historic Preservation (NTHP) announced the creation of the Historic Preservation Defense Fund today during the 2026 National Preservation Summit.

It is aimed at protecting "the nation's historic places and the laws that safeguard them against urgent threats emanating from Washington", according to NTHP.

"Through the Historic Preservation Defense Fund, the National Trust recognizes the magnitude of the crisis facing us today. And we stand ready to protect what's at stake," said NTHP president Brent Leggs.

"It will provide resources for legal defense, public advocacy, and community action when historic places and the laws that protect them are under threat."

NTHP has been involved in lawsuits over the government's architectural interventions in DC, including a suit to block changes at the White House, which resulted in a ban that was recently lifted.

It said the decision to launch the fund stems from a change in the federal government's approach to preservation.

"Once, we looked to the federal government as a foundational partner in the preservation of the American story," said Leggs.

"We had a shared understanding, even if from different sides of the aisle or cultural contexts, that saving our historical record mattered."

"But as the government divests from this work, it is up to us to take up this charge in earnest."

Trump has denounced the NTHP as "bad for our country".

Read:

Saarinen's Dulles terminal set to be enveloped by Trump-backed airport

On its website, NTHP named The White House East Wing and the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts as evidence of federal preservation safeguards being "in jeopardy".

The site of the now-demolished East Wing is currently a construction zone to make way for president Donald Trump's in-progress ballroom extension, and the Kennedy Center recently shut down due to a battle over Trump's plans to rename and renovate it

It also cited the government's proposed Triumphal Arch as an "intrusion" on historic sightlines in Washington DC.

Leggs spoke to the federal government's attempts to rewrite Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider the effects their projects have on historic US properties.

Currently, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation (ACHP) is seeking to weaken Section 106 regulations, according to NPR.

Read:

How Donald Trump is using architecture to reshape Washington DC

Leggs said if implemented, the new rules could "dramatically diminish" current legal protections around projects such as the Reflecting Pool and the Smithsonian, both of which have also faced changes under Trump.

"The American public is demanding change and is impatient to see accountability from Congress, the Courts, and the Administration to ensure that no one can violate or weaponize policy to endanger these places," he said.

"It is not an exaggeration to say that this moment is existential."

The National Trust for Historic Preservation is a privately funded nonprofit founded in 1949 and chartered by US Congress to uphold standards in preservation.

Architectural historian Brent Leggs was appointed as NTHP president in June and is the first African American CEO to lead the NTHP.

item.content:encoded:
Car brand Bentley has revealed the Torcal, its first fully electric car. Ahead of its unveiling today, we spoke to design director Robin Page about how the car balances an electric future with the brand's heritage.

Unveiled today at a launch event in London, the Torcal is a fully electric SUV – the first fully electric vehicle by the luxury car company.

Unlike other luxury car brands – most notably Ferrari and Jaguar – Bentley has not radically overhauled the shape for its first electric vehicle.

According to Page, this was to create an electric car that was clearly modern, but also recognisable as a Bentley.

Page told Dezeen his team began talking about direction four years ago.

"That was when we asked, 'Are we doing a car dedicated to an electric language, or should we do another great Bentley with a more modern language – not directly focused on electrification?'"

"We decided that our best route would be to embrace our heritage and DNA, but in a modern, progressive way."

The Torcal has a long wheelbase with a form that evokes previous Bentleys. Page explained that this form stemmed from Bentley's design principles rather than aerodynamic concerns related to electrification.

"With electrification, what mainly drives the form's language is the aerodynamics and the package proportion – aerodynamics directly relates to range," he said.

"The laws of aerodynamics start to give you quite a moulded form and a certain tail, but we decided that aerodynamics shouldn't lead the design. What's dominated the shape is our design principles, and they are based on our DNA and heritage."

The Torcal takes stylistic cues from previous Bentleys, including a continuous bonnet line, expressed rear arches and a prominent grill.

"Outright elegance, the iconic grill, the endless bonnet line, the resting beast – they're our principles, and we've let them dominate the design rather than aerodynamics," said Page.

Although aerodynamics didn't drive the design, Page highlighted the vehicle's range of 600 kilometres.

The grill, inessential in an electric car, is still clearly expressed.

As with the overall design of the car, Bentley nodded to the past. It referenced the grill of the Continental T, but with a modern twist – it can be illuminated in a diamond pattern.

Page said the team decided it needed a grill and that closing it off would feel "like a hand over a mouth", opting for what it considers an art piece.

"[We] decided to celebrate it, to do a piece of art with light," said Paige.

At the launch, the Torcal was presented in a light, yellowy green, another modern update to the brand's heritage.

"The Bentley green is a much darker, solid green," said Page. "We wanted a colour that showed the form, something a bit lighter, this colour works pretty well."

Inside, the car has a wing-shaped dash and natural materials including timber and Merino wool. It has a modestly sized screen – for a high-end car – and numerous physical dials.

"We didn't want to go down the clinical, super modern material route, because you end up with this quite stark, cold feeling inside," said Page.

"It really captures a place you want to be, rather than something you look at and think, 'that's modern'. It needs to be something that feels fresh, but feels comfortable."

Bentley said its choice to make its first electric car an SUV will open up a new market and offer something that other luxury car brands are not doing.

"The reason we're all doing SUVs is that it's a growing market," he said. "We've had a lot of comments from customers who say they could use this Bentley every day."

When it goes on sale later this year, the Torcal will be the first Bentley to feature the brand's redesigned logo, which was revealed last year.

item.content:encoded:
Alaska-based artist Nicholas Galanin has created a metal sculpture resembling a stretched animal hide in front of the St Louis Gateway Arch to challenge "narratives of westward expansion" for art festival Counterpublic.

Land is Never a Gateway (Sightline/Lifeline) is located in front of the Eero Saarinen-designed monument, on a small sidewalk plot. From there, visitors can crouch down and look up at the piece, which is meant to create an optical illusion with the gateway.

When viewed from below, the sculpture resembles animal hide stretched across the arch, transforming it visually from a monument into a hide-processing frame.

Galanin created the piece to challenge the narratives surrounding the ideologies of Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny, movements under which colonial settlers, ranchers and the US government began to migrate past the Mississippi River and into the western United States beginning in the early 1800s.

Eero Saarinen's Gateway Arch, a grand, 630-foot-tall ( 94-metre-tall) swooping structure located on the banks of the Mississippi River, was designed as a monument to Westward expansion and is referred to as "The Gateway to the West" in popular culture.

"The work developed through thinking about the Gateway Arch and the narratives of westward expansion it monumentalizes," Galanin told Dezeen. "I wanted to interrupt that sightline."

"That alignment is both a sightline and a lifeline: a reminder that perspective determines which histories are visible and which have been obscured."

Read:

Torkwase Dyson fuses sound and architecture for St Louis installation

Galanin, who is based in Sitka, Alaska and is of local Lingit and Unangax̂ descent, was informed by visits to St Louis for the piece, where he researched local history as part of the commission for Counterpublic.

Specifically, he examined "the histories held in the land itself" and "Indigenous dispossession, racial capitalism, segregation, and extraction," he told Dezeen.

Processing a hide, or animal skin, is a traditional art practised by many Native American and First Nations people. One step in the lengthy process involves tying the hide to a frame to stretch and cure it, which is pictured in Galanin's sculpture.

Galanin often explores "adaptation, resilience, survival, active cultural amnesia, dream, memory, cultural resurgence, connection to and disconnection from the land" through his work, according to his artist statement. 

The third edition of the Counterpublic brings together local and global artists to create commissioned pieces and works around the city.

This year's festival, Coyote Time, invited artists to explore the history, present and future of St Louis, and included installations by artists such as Oglála Lakȟóta artist Kite and Los Angeles-based artist Alice Bucknell among fifty others.

It is led by executive director James McAnally and assistant curator Charlie Farrell, with guest curation by Jordan Carterm, Rapheal Fonesca, Stefanie Hessler, Nora N Khan and Wanda Nandibush.

In 2023, New York artist Torkwase Dyson designed a monolithic black structure that highlighted the ragtime music of American composer Scott Joplin for the event.

The photography is by Jon Gitchoff, courtesy of Counterpublic

Counterpublic runs from 10 September to 12 December. For more architecture, design and art events across the world, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a centre dedicated to nuclear learning set within the historic landscape of Stowe, UK, is among the projects by students at Cardiff University.

Also included is an ecology centre designed around the transparency of its AI use, and a community-driven recycling centre that gives unwanted items a second life.

Cardiff University

Institution: Cardiff University
School: Welsh School of Architecture
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)

School statement:

"The Welsh School of Architecture (WSA), based in Cardiff, is a world-renowned institution for design and built environment studies.

"Originally founded over a century ago, the WSA has a strong tradition of excellence in architectural education; our teaching and research embrace the diversity and transdisciplinary nature of architecture.

"We foster curious, creative, critical, ethical learners who can approach challenges with wide-ranging, flexible skills and knowledge.

"Our vision is to contribute to the making of built environments that enhance the well-being of current and future generations while caring for the planet.

"The Master in Architecture (MArch) is a two-year programme. Accredited by RIBA, ARB and LAM (Malaysia), the programme encourages students to forge a personal stance informed by critical, reflective, creative and interdisciplinary approaches to design.

"In the first year of the MArch – the year of education in practice – our students undertake academic and project work while based in paid employment in an architectural practice.

"The second year, by contrast, is spent entirely in the school. Here, students develop grounded but research-led study through a dissertation and design thesis, whilst also undertaking studies in the practice, management and economics of architecture.

"Through the design thesis, each student initially identifies a site and topic for exploration that is framed within the context of a thematic design unit.

"They go on to use design as a vehicle for research and the development of imaginative architectural propositions."

A New Garden City: Exploring the limits of Densification and Quality within a Pre-established Neighbourhood by Ruby Staple

"A Garden City for Tomorrow proposes a densification and decarbonisation framework for Ely and Caerau, providing 103 new PassivHaus homes while upgrading existing ones to EnerPhit standards.

"The prototype tests how far density can increase without reducing housing quality, balancing sustainability, spatial beautification and community needs.

"The scheme proposes improved thermal performance and expansion of housing through active community engagement, which would ensure future strategies better reflect local priorities.

"Overall, it offers a provocation for low-carbon, socially connected neighbourhood design beyond budget-driven mass housing."

Student: Ruby Staple
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutors: Mhairi McVicar and Dan Benham
Email: rubiestaple[at]gmail.com

Building Futures by Éabha Strong-Wright

"This timber skills centre explores how architecture can create opportunities for young people through participation and connection to place.

"Located on the edge of an ancient woodland, the thesis transforms existing community and environmental assets, with a focus on construction and learning.

"Guided by a zero-waste design philosophy, it utilises site-sourced materials, focusing on roundwood construction and using every part of a tree. An experimental wood-fibre composite connector transforms workshop waste into a structural system.

"The proposal combines retrofit, landscape intervention and new construction to reconnect the community with the woodland while creating opportunities for long-term education and employment."

Student: Éabha Strong-Wright
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutors: Mhairi McVicar and Dan Benham
Email: eabhasw02[at]gmail.com

Cybernetic Ecology by Maisy Sykes

"Cybernetic Ecology explores how architecture can create a regenerative relationship between people, nature and technology.

"Located within the flood-prone landscape of Cumberland Basin, Bristol, the project reimagines the European headquarters of biotech company Insilico Medicine as a workplace for AI-driven ecological research and public engagement.

"Five climate-controlled biomes cultivate medicinal plants, while AI-controlled moving roofs and adaptive facades respond to changing environmental conditions.

"Principles of transparency expose hidden systems, from visible laboratories to AI server rooms where waste heat supports the building. The project makes artificial intelligence visible, understandable, and accessible to the public."

Student: Maisy Sykes
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutors: Lawrence Duck and Shankari Raj
Email: maisy.sykes[at]icloud.com

The Architecture Collective by Ollie Yelland

"As the built environment sector has become increasingly complex and hyper-specialised, the architect's role has fragmented, creating an industry where large corporate firms hold a distinct advantage.

"This thesis proposes a new collective framework designed to empower small architecture practices by cross-programming the fragmented disciplines of the construction industry.

"Drawing organisational inspiration from large practices and architectural schools, the project culminates in a collaborative professional hub located in Cardiff Bay.

"Deliberately situated away from the city centre's mega-firms, this spatial intervention provides a shared ecosystem for architects and allied professionals to pool resources, innovate, and reclaim industry agency."

Student: Ollie Yelland
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutors: Mark Hillier and Yasser Megahed
Email: ollieyelland[at]gmail.com

Below the Surface: Reimagining Competitive Sailing Infrastructure as a Mediator Between People and Performance by William Underwood

"The elite sailing industry often keeps people and place at an arm's length. It presents the sport as a spectacle to be admired from a distance, celebrating the product's performance over the people and processes that make it possible.

"In response, this project explores the concept of permeability, questioning how sport STEM centres might reimagine themselves as civic destinations without compromising competitive advantages or R+D secrecy.

"Through strategic voids and public cross-programming, the proposal creates an open, permeable centre, blurring public and private realms, allowing visitors to witness the inner workings of STEM activity through the lens of competitive sailing."

Student: William Underwood
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutors: Yasser Megahed and Mark Hillier
Email: waunderwood[at]hotmail.co.uk

Cultivated Dwelling by Martha Spencer Jones

"This thesis re-imagines the abandoned Mid Wales Hospital as a place of cultivation and renewed human-nature interdependency, where gathering becomes the central driver for re-dwelling.

"Black Mountains College, young families, local farmers and the Talgarth community form a shared campus where regenerative farming, experimental growing, and communal workshops create a living framework for ecological learning.

"Grounded in primitive notions of dwelling, the thesis explores how historic forms of gathering can be repurposed, so that humans and nature can co-exist holistically.

"By reframing dereliction as opportunity, the project proposes a rural regeneration model that fosters climate resilience and interdependent living grounded in gathering."

Student: Martha Spencer Jones
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutor: Marga Munar Bauza
Email: marthaspencerjones[at]gmail.com

Somnath: Waste to Worth by Huriyyah Aiba Binti Nur Malek

"Today, the world is generating waste at a rate beyond its ability to sustainably manage it. Driven by population growth, rapid urbanisation, rising incomes and increasing consumption, cities face growing environmental and social challenges.

"Based in Somnath, India, the catalyst project proposes a community-driven recycling centre that gives unwanted items a second life, converts food waste into biogas, and treats wastewater for reuse.

"The proposal seeks to redefine perceptions of waste by transforming discarded materials into valuable resources that can be re-integrated into everyday life, reducing their impacts on our environment while fostering community participation and a more sustainable future."

Student: Huriyyah Aiba Binti Nur Malek
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutor: Shibu Raman
Email: aibamalek[at]gmail.com

Ty Lles: Cardiff University's Home for Women's Wellbeing by Ella Coomer

"Tŷ Lles: Cardiff University's Home for Women's Wellbeing explores how architecture can address barriers women face in sport and movement.

"Situated within Cardiff University's campus, the project reimagines the sports facility as a holistic environment focused on care, wellbeing and community.

"The scheme positions architecture as a catalyst for empowerment and participation organised around four hubs: community, movement, wellbeing and health.

"The design supports physical activity, mental wellbeing, healthcare and social connection, defined by a sculptural timber gridshell canopy and organic forms, to create inclusive and calming spaces rooted in collective care principles."

Student: Ella Coomer
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutor: Hiral Patel
Email: ellacoomer[at]icloud.com

The Second Draft of Yesterday by Kenneth Dhillon

"The Second Draft of Yesterday confronts a building suspended between intention and completion: Herzog and de Meuron's Berlin Modern M20, frozen in construction at the Kulturforum, severing the civic dialogue between Mies van der Rohe's Neue Nationalgalerie and Scharoun's Philharmonie.

"The project asks what an architect's obligation is to an unfinished building, and answers through editorial intervention. Selected structural bays are erased to create civic porosity.

"The retained fabric becomes the ground; the erased voids become civic space. A copper facade records time, and a rotating brick Palimpsest Tower turns the building's logic inward. The pathological becomes propelling."

Student: Kenneth Dhillon
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutor: Alexis Germanos
Email: kennethdhillon[at]outlook.com

Deterritorializing the Railway Station, a Flâneur's Architectural Dream by Anastasia Stachtiari

"Small-to-medium railway stations make up around 80 per cent of the UK's rail network, yet remain underinvested. This thesis addresses this overlooked typology through an ecology of rail travel rooted in Wales.

"Drawing on situationist theory, it develops the concept of rail psychogeography, experienced through the lens of the flâneur, in which the railway journey becomes an experience of drift and discovery.

"The project challenges the present conventional typology, which is driven primarily by operational efficiency, arguing that the urban presence and architectural, social and civic value of small-to-medium railway stations are often underestimated.

"It asks how their components might be reimagined to support unconventional uses of platforms, kinetic crossings and flexible programmes that encourage lingering, wandering and exploration within stations and throughout the rail journey."

Student: Anastasia Stachtiari
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutor: Will Judge
Email: anastasia.stachtiari[at]gmail.com

Reviving the People's Floodplain by Catherine Towers

"Located on the Severn Ham floodplain in Tewkesbury, the project proposes a flood-responsive civic and ecological landscape that occupies, rather than resists, seasonal flooding.

"A linear intervention, the Mowing Edge, separates a public commons and water-treatment landscape from restored floodplain meadow and wetland habitats, while functioning as resilient community infrastructure.

"At the threshold between Tewkesbury and the Severn Ham, elevated walkways, floating structures and adaptable public spaces remain accessible throughout changing water levels, supporting ecological restoration, environmental education, year-round recreational uses and flood resilience.

"The proposal reimagines flooding as a civic asset, transforming periods of inundation from disruption into opportunities for occupation, learning and engagement with the historically important landscape."

Student: Catherine Towers
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutors: Andrew Carr and Reishin Kunishima Watabe
Email: catherinetowers22[at]gmail.com

Learning in the Landscape by Amelia Farman

"Learning in the Landscape reimagines nuclear energy as civic architecture within the Oxford–Cambridge Arc.

"Responding to the rapid growth of artificial intelligence and its escalating energy demands, the project proposes a Centre of Nuclear Learning set within the historic landscape of Stowe.

"Drawing on the tradition of the English landscape garden and the villa as a place of intellectual exchange, the proposal combines research, education and public engagement.

"This thesis challenges the defensive image of nuclear energy, arguing instead for an integrated, culturally grounded masterplan that supports both technological advancement and civic identity."

Student: Amelia Farman
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutor: Tim Burton
Email: ameliafarman[at]gmail.com

item.content:encoded:
Mexican lighting designer Federico Stefanovich has worked with local interiors firm Nama Studio to renovate his studio in a hotel-turned-arts building in Mexico City's Centro neighbourhood.

Known for his expressive metal lighting, Federico Stefanovich renovated the interior of the balcony-clad Edificio Humboldt, a historic building designed by Canadian architect Thomas Sinclair Gore and completed in 1922.

Today it holds dozens of art and design studios and workshops.

Stefanovich and Nama Studio carefully preserved the historic details while adding rich colours and textures to showcase Stefanovich's designs and provide working space. It serves as a studio, showroom and production workshop.

"The balconies were one of the elements I immediately fell in love with when I first saw the space," Stefanovich told Dezeen.

"The large original windows, which open completely onto the balconies, had already been carefully restored before our intervention, preserving details from the 1920s, including their handles and iron latches."

Visitors enter the studio area via a seating area with showcase shelving that leads out into the long, main space with a lounge area at one end and a long table for displaying goods on the other.

In this primary showroom area, Edificio Humboldt's windows bring in plenty of natural light – which can present a problem for showcasing lighting designs.

To get around this and take full advantage of the light-filled rooms, panels were added to create backdrops for the lights, including a custom-designed modular panel system with metal poles interspersed with wooden blocks supporting them on the edges.

The panel's blue colour was created by layering tones almost like a limewash.

"I would describe it as a muted mineral blue, with a slightly weathered quality," said Stefanovich. "We wanted the colour to have depth and variation rather than read as a completely flat or uniform surface."

"The perimeter panel system is interrupted by the windows, creating a rhythm between the new architectural elements and the historic structure."

In the main space, this "muted mineral blue" is complemented by chocolate-toned plaster and brown-stained wood in the furniture, pedestals and wainscotting.

Aged flooring hints at the age of the building.

The lounge area, completely lined by the blue panel system, features a semi-circular sofa custom-made by Stefanovich's team.

Running along the elongated showroom is another panelling system. Instead of blue, the team opted for fibreglass that is yellowy and opaque but translucent enough to let light through, reminiscent of Japanese washi paper.

These fibreglass panels are part of a sliding door system that reveals the workshop area with utilitarian elements such as plywood furniture, MDF panels and steel storage racks.

Overall, Stefanovich said that the space was meant to reference his design style directly, which he described as ornate but not overly so.

Read:

JSa transforms Mexican factory for its own architecture studio

"There is a subtle mid-century quality to the space, combined with handmade processes and certain more expressive, almost baroque gestures," he said.

"The intention was to bring these references together in a contemporary way, creating an environment that feels sophisticated but not overly formal, and that allows the architecture and my pieces to exist as part of the same language."

For the opening of the studio, Stefanovich collaborated with gallery Ago Projects to display his Salina Collection. The designer said the fibreglass in the studio space references the fibreglass of the collection.

Other self-designed studios include Jasmine Fisher's atmospheric studio in London and Victoria Yakusha's studio with a "living island" in Miami.

The photography is by Alejandro Ramirez Orozco.

Dezeen Showroom: carefully tailored leather upholstery takes centre stage in the Nyla executive chair, produced by furniture brand Omidi.

Bringing the feeling of a private office wherever it sits, the Nyla leather chair combines a high back, leather upholstery and advanced adjustment controls smoothly integrated into its aluminium alloy base.

Omidi created the Nyla leather chair out of the belief that true luxury lies not in excess but in refinement, striving to reduce the chair to a clean and balanced silhouette while centring the capability of leather to develop unique character and make an item feel more personal over time.

"Omidi's leather executive chair collection focuses on combining refined craftsmanship with modern comfort, offering designs suitable for both professional offices and luxury home workspaces," said the company.

A Gold winner in the MUSE Design Awards, the chair includes integrated armrests to support a natural body position and a sculpted seat made from high-density foam that provides firmness and resilience.

The adjustment mechanisms include a gas lift system certified for up to 136 kilograms, 135-degree multi-angle tilt and a sliding seat, while lumbar support supports the natural curve of the spine and reduced pressure on the back over prolonged periods of sitting.

item.content:encoded:
Scottish architecture studio Pend has expanded and updated a Georgian townhouse in Edinburgh, complementing its existing pale stone exterior with an extension clad in skinny red bricks.

Named Newhaven after its location in the Newhaven Conservation Area, the extension was designed to improve the connection between the home and its garden.

Pend said the house had previously suffered from a raised, compartmentalised front and a neglected conservatory and shed to the rear.

In response, the Edinburgh-based studio created a new secondary entrance into the home via a single-storey brick extension, providing direct access into a new living area that leads straight through to the dining space and central kitchen.

"The existing entrance is positioned one level above the kitchen as a result of the site's topography, meaning that visitors entered into a sequence of more private rooms before reaching the main living spaces," project architect Joanna Hobbs told Dezeen.

"The proposal introduces a more legible secondary entrance from the rear, creating a direct route into the kitchen and principal entertaining spaces while allowing the existing entrance to retain a more private function," she added. "We worked from the kitchen outwards, widening existing openings to draw more light into the centre of the house and establish longer sight-lines towards the garden."

The extension's design takes cues from the curved masonry walls of the existing home. Over time, these walls have been repaired with brickwork infills, which informed the skinny red bricks used for Newhaven's external walls.

Inside, the form of the curving stone wall is referenced in a circular skylight, a curved timber opening between the dining and living space and curved shelves tucked into the extension's corners.

"The existing rear elevation is defined by a curved wall constructed in solid sandstone masonry, in places more than 3ft thick," Hobbs said.

"The unusual geometry distinguishes the property from its neighbours and became an important reference point for the design, informing a series of curved elements within the new intervention and landscape," she added.

Read:

Stone walls form "strong yet subtle" cottage extension in Scotland

Tucked alongside the new entrance is a small study, offering a quiet space away from the main social areas that overlooks the garden through a porthole-like window.

These motifs also continue through into the garden, where a snaking path divides the existing space into two zones – a more informal lawn area and a paved terrace lined by a curving brick-lined bed with steps up to the side access gate.

Based in Leith, Edinburgh, Pend was founded in 2021 by Jamie Anderson with a focus on residential projects.

Previous projects by the studio include the extension of a heritage-listed Georgian farmhouse in East Lothian with new volumes in fluted pink-toned stonework, and the transformation of an overlooked infill site into a series of mews homes in Edinburgh.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen Showroom: Italian brand Tubes and designer Elisa Ossino bring an echo of the workshop tool board to heating design with their electric Grid radiator.

Taking the form of a thin panel of perforated aluminium, Grid combines "tidiness, aesthetic modularity and minimal rigour", according to Tubes.

Its geometric surface turns the radiator into an architectural element while serving as an attachment point for optional accessories like shelves or hooks – a feature that is particularly practical in the bathroom.

"The object is a reinvented everyday ritual, where warmth meets geometric elegance," said Ossino. "Minimalism, functionality and personality coexist in a project designed for those seeking distinctive contemporary design."

Grid's deceptively simple design involved the creation of new manufacturing equipment that could achieve the softened, controlled indentation of the cut-out circles.

The radiator is made of recycled and recyclable aluminium, entirely from an Italian supply chain, and is available in a choice of 140 RAL colours.

Grid's catalogue of accessories includes hooks, shelves, towel rails and, for the first time, a small mirror.

item.content:encoded:
Paranoia over so-called "teen takeovers" ignores the fundamental problem: that our cities have left young people with nowhere to go, writes Christopher Martin.

America this summer acquired the phrase "teen takeover". Large gatherings of young people, organised online, appearing in downtowns, malls and parks.

Some involved violence and yes, plainly these incidents require a response. But the phrase itself is revealing.

Perhaps before asking what is wrong with these gatherings, we should ask a more uncomfortable question

Takeover. As though young people appearing en masse in the centre of their own city constitutes a territorial incursion.

London had its own version this spring, and across Europe, anxiety about youth alienation, political disengagement and unrest is growing.

A recent academic paper calls the way cities respond to young people the "patronising city", highlighting that young people are tolerated in public space principally when supervised, consuming or behaving according to adult expectations.

Read:

MIT finds people walking faster and lingering less in public space

So perhaps before asking what is wrong with these gatherings, we should ask a more uncomfortable question: where did we expect young people to go?

Disappearing youth clubs, the library that no longer opens late, the cheap cafe that is now a chain, the recreation ground, the shopping arcade, the public bench, and the ordinary bit of city in which nobody particularly minded if you spent an afternoon doing nothing. All gone.

These "third spaces" – neither home, nor school or work, but the informal spaces between them – are where relationships form and social life happens. For young people, they are particularly important because home and school are not really theirs. They generally do not own property, are too young for bars and often lack the money required to participate in an increasingly commercial urban culture.

The contemporary city has become remarkably intolerant of people without obvious economic purpose

Axios reported this summer that the disappearance of malls and affordable hangouts, combined with public spaces that frequently feel hostile to teenagers, is leaving American teenagers with fewer places to gather.

The resulting mass meet-ups are then treated as evidence of the problem rather than, perhaps, evidence of the demand. We remove the places where young people can gather in small groups, then panic when they gather in large ones. There is a wonderful circularity to this.

The contemporary city has become remarkably intolerant of people without obvious economic purpose. Pavements must move pedestrians. Kerbs must load or charge something. Squares need events. Walls carry advertising. Parks acquire cafes. Railway concourses funnel passengers past retail with more enthusiasm than they guide them onto trains.

Read:

Study finds swathes of England left with "public toilet deserts" as facilities decline

Connected to this is the issue we have, as adult society, with loitering. There are few words in the municipal vocabulary more suspicious than loitering. Nobody describes an elderly couple sitting outside a cafe in Rome as loitering. They are participating.

Loitering is what other people do. More precisely, it is what people without obvious economic purpose do.

Artist Nils Norman began documenting the architecture of this anxiety in the 1990s. His Contemporary Picturesque recorded the studs, barriers and small devices appearing in increasingly managed and privatised city centres. While the original picturesque gave us ruins, grottoes and serpentine lakes, the contemporary version gives us stainless-steel knobs attached to a granite ledge so that a 15-year-old cannot grind a skateboard along it. One civilisation built follies. Ours builds anti-follies.

We worry about screen time while removing the reasons to leave the screen

And the skateboard stud is more interesting than it looks. Its entire purpose is to prevent somebody finding an unintended pleasure in an object.

Skateboarders read architecture incorrectly. A staircase becomes an event. A handrail becomes recreational equipment. A ledge becomes a playground. They refuse the instruction manual set out by future generations, precisely as young people should.

This built environment, hostile to young people, is exactly what is being questioned by groups like Bristol-based campaigners Playing Out, saying Yes to Ball Games.

Read:

"The St George's cross speaks of the power of design to transform public space"

We worry about screen time while removing the reasons to leave the screen. We fret about social skills while closing third spaces. We complain that teenagers organise their lives through Snapchat and TikTok, then treat their physical arrival in the city as a public-order incident.

Apparently, we would like young people to spend less time online, provided they don't turn up anywhere. This is where the public realm stops being a discussion about paving materials and becomes something considerably more important.

The Council of Europe's new charter on youth participation says young people require the "means, space and structures" to participate in society. Space is not metaphorical. Democracy does not begin when somebody turns 18 and receives a polling card.

If we want young people to participate in society, society needs to find somewhere for them to participate

It is rehearsed through years of occupying shared places, encountering strangers, negotiating behaviour and discovering that other people are both fascinating and tremendously irritating. The public realm is where we learn to live with people we didn't choose.

This makes London's transformation of Oxford Street timely. One of the world's most commercial streets is now beginning its most significant reinvention in generations. Through this, Oxford Street can demonstrate that commercial success and civic generosity are not opposites; that one of Europe's great shopping streets can also provide something increasingly scarce in prosperous cities: space with no entry price and no instruction manual.

It matters far beyond London. Cities everywhere are worried about young people's alienation, their relationship with democracy, their social skills, their mental health and the amount of their lives disappearing into screens. Perhaps we should stop treating these as entirely separate problems.

If we want young people to participate in society, society needs to find somewhere for them to participate. A city that makes room for its young is not surrendering control. It is investing in its future.

Christopher Martin is co-founder and managing director of Urban Movement.

item.content:encoded:
Design firm Yont Studio has used salvaged car seats and more than 140 cassette tapes to create an analogue sound installation inside Berlin department store KaDeWe.

Created in collaboration with Telekom Electronic Beats and local fashion brand Namilia, the installation is set on the second floor of the city's century-old department store, which was recently renovated by OMA.

The hybrid display stand and listening booth aims to take Berliners on a sonic ride down memory lane.

The collaboration was inspired by the 1977 Iggy Pop song The Passenger, which he recorded during his time in West Berlin with David Bowie, describing the sweet melancholy of watching the world pass by through a car window.

To evoke this same feeling, Yont Studio created a circle of second-hand black leather car seats, inviting shoppers to slow down and settle in with a pair of headphones, so they can listen to a selection of rare and second-hand cassettes.

"It comes almost from a place of nostalgia; the memory of listening to your favourite singer's cassette on a road trip as a kid," said Coşan Karadeniz, who founded Yont Studio together with Serdar Ayvaz. "Contrary to today's internet world, it's a slow and physical ritual."

The installation was designed to mark the launch of a collaborative fashion collection created by Namilia, run by Royal College of Art graduates Nan Li and Emilia Pfohl, music platform Telekom Electronic Beats and British indie rock band Wet Leg.

To display the pieces from the collection and hold the cassette players and tapes, Yont Studio created a quartet of bright-pink foam wedges, with integrated metal shelving and clothes rails.

The duo distressed the foam by hitting it with stones and burning it with flamethrowers and it was completed with metal rebar poking out of the polystyrene.

"It's really fun because it's an intuitive process," Ayvaz said. "It's quite manual, very Stone Age."

Read:

OMA adds wood-clad escalators to KaDeWe department store in Berlin

The aim was to evoke the brutalist concrete birthplaces of Berlin techno. At the same time, playful details like the glossy pink car paint and clothes hooks shaped like butt plugs bring moments of irreverence.

"Namilia's fashion attitude was quite a starting point for us – unapologetic, kinky, queer," Ayvaz explained.

"KaDeWe is a place with a really rich history; it's the first luxury department store in Berlin," he added. "And we were really happy to bring something very young, fresh, and in a way provocative."

Techno can also be found in the cassette collection itself, which includes sets by pioneering DJs like Sven Väth and Carl Cox, alongside little-known world music.

"There is a lot of music that I'm so sure you can't find on Spotify or anywhere else because it's just super niche or it was only recorded once," said the Telekom Electronic Beats team, who compiled the selection from second-hand shops and private collectors.

"There is a lot of music that was recorded from the radio, entire sets that someone just recorded. So you can basically only hear them here."

The listening booth is open until 27 September, with visitors encouraged to stay and listen for as long as they want.

"We encourage people to bring their cassettes and listen to whatever they want, or maybe exchange what they have there," Karadeniz said. "So it's kind of like a living organism."

Karadeniz and Ayvaz, two club kids who met while studying architecture at the Technical University Berlin, have found a niche in catering to the growing demand for well-designed music spaces.

The duo are known for creating playful brutalist DJ booths using their distinctive epoxy-foam combination, previously seen at this year's Milan design week and in a record store they designed in Berlin's Mitte district.

"We are getting more and more digitised, so people actually care more about sensual experiences," Ayvaz said. "Sound is one of the first things you notice when you're in a space. So I think people will care more and more about being physically in a place and experiencing that."

item.content:encoded:
Tech brand Apple has revealed the 600-seat Apple Music Hall, its first live music venue, which sits alongside its offices within London's Battersea Power Station.

Set to open later this year, the venue overlooks the power station's Turbine A at the northern end of the huge brick building. It will be Apple's first permanent performance venue.

Designed by Apple's in-house team led by Apple Places vice president Kristina Raspe, the venue takes its industrial language directly from the Giles Gilbert Scott-designed power station.

The venue is flanked by brick walls, while the building's huge structural steel joists are exposed at the rear of the performance space.

Read:

Apple reveals Battersea Power Station store as latest "evolution of the Apple Store"

As a nod to the art deco design of the original power station, a series of four illuminated, streamline-styled arches span the venue.

Bronze, art deco balconies were placed between the arches, as box-like areas overlooking the main venue space.

According to Apple, the flexible venue was designed to give artists an "unprecedented level of creative control".

The venue has an 11.5-metre-wide stage and can be arranged in multiple configurations as either an all-seated or all-standing venue, or a combination of the two.

Music will be played through a 48-speaker spatial sound system, while 16 hardwired cameras can capture performances to be broadcast.

"In short, an artist can perform an intimate live show for fans at Apple Music Hall and walk out with a finished Spatial Audio recording, a broadcast-ready mix, and multicamera video — all from a single show," said Apple.

Alongside the main venue space is what Apple describes as a "full production facility" that contains a pair of professional-standard recording and mix studios.

The venue also includes a dedicated space for Apple's radio station – Apple Music Radio, which will now broadcast from inside the building.

Apple Music Hall was built alongside Apple's Foster + Partners-designed European HQ, which occupies the centre of Battersea Power Station. One of London's best-known buildings, the power station was refurbished in 2022 by architecture studio WilkinsonEyre after being derelict for 40 years.

It now contains apartments on the upper floors, with restaurants and shops, including an Apple Store in the former turbine halls.

item.content:encoded:
Furniture brand Karimoku has opened Oyado Mas, an exhibition of furniture and accessories by its Mas label, showcased in an environment designed to resemble an inn complete with a reception and guest room.

Karimoku's Mas brand, which makes products using Japanese woods, provided the furniture for the exhibition, located in the Karimoku Commons Tokyo showroom in the city's Aoyama neighbourhood.

The company also presented designs by a number of other Japanese brands, most of which it previously collaborated with in the Japanmade Vol 1 exhibition for Copenhagen design week 3 Days of Design.

The exhibition features lighting by New Light Pottery, washi paper by Nao Tesuki Washi, tableware by Sekisaka, candles by Sheep and bedding by Sinso.

The furniture and accessories were combined to create what Karimoku describes as "an imaginary oyado", or Japanese inn, designed to convey a sense of comfort to visitors.

Visitors enter Oyado Mas through a noren, a Japanese fabric divider that is usually used at the entrance of inns.

At the start of the exhibition, they are welcomed by an area designed to resemble the reception of an inn, which also has a shop that sells smaller pieces from the exhibition.

The front area also includes a small lounge furnished with Mas chairs.

The showroom then opens up into a second exhibition space designed as the guestroom of the inn, complete with a bedroom and living room area.

The idea of showcasing the furniture in a more residential setting than usual came about as Mas now has a focus on designs with a distinctly Japanese feel.

"From this year, MAS has adopted 'New Japanese Comfort' as a phrase that embodies our brand," Mas design director Wataru Kumano told Dezeen.

Read:

Seven exhibitions that showcased Japanese design in Copenhagen

"In addition to the ergonomic comfort expected of furniture, we aim to let users experience a sense of comfort that can be felt through the background of materials unique to Japan and highly developed woodworking techniques," he continued.

At Oyado Mas, the brand also aimed to underline the hospitality experience by serving tea made from plants found in Japanese forests, as well as sweets.

According to Kumano, oyados are especially associated with Japan and quite different from hotels, which made the theme suitable for Mas' furniture's new concept.

Among the pieces that will be on sale in the showroom are a new fragrance by Mas and Sheep, a spoon by Sekisaka and Mas' WK Stool.

"We believe that the setting of an 'oyado' provides an ideal context in which to embody this new brand concept," Kumano said.

"By creating an 'oyado' spatial experience that cannot be fully expressed through furniture alone, together with Japanese lighting, tea, food, paper, tools, fragrance and textiles, we hope to create a place that stimulates the creation of new values through objects," he continued.

Mas chose the brands that are taking part in Oyado Mas as it had worked with most of them previously and thought they would create items suitable for the inn experience.

"We invited these brands and makers because they embody elements essential to the future of Japanese oyado experiences," Kumano said.

"With the exception of Sinso, we also exhibited alongside them at this year's 3 Days of Design, where we found that they share the same values as Mas."

Karimoku has previously focused on wood in its The Age of Wood exhibition, which was created together with Danish design duo Christian + Jade.

item.content:encoded:
Photographer Gurpreet Chawla has captured this year's architectural installations at the annual Burning Man festival in Nevada, from a broken Eiffel Tower to a chapel made from nylon panels.

Teams of artists, architects and volunteers installed creative installations for the yearly gathering in Nevada's alkaline desert.

The installations and pavilions need to be relatively lightweight, as they must be shipped in and completely shipped out in line with Burning Man's leave-nothing-behind policy.

Many of the volunteer teams that build the structures choose wood, and several of the installations are burned at the end of the festival alongside the yearly temple and effigy – or Man Base pavilion – the only structures organised directly by the Burning Man team.

Read:

Twelve installations designed by architects at Burning Man over the years

Burning Man draws intense emotions from participants. For the designer of this year's Man Base Pavilion, Alexander Rose, it marked his 30th trip to the temporary Black Rock City.

Rose said he was designing the pavilion at the same time as his mother was on her deathbed.

"My submission for the Man Base Pavilion came about while I was sitting with my mother in her last weeks of life," he told Dezeen.

"My mom finding out that we had won the design award just days before her passing makes this design one of the most important projects I have ever worked on."

On top of the emotional aspect of the event, the weather in the desert, called the Playa by festival-goers, can be unforgiving. This year, high winds and concern over local fires gave the builders an extra dimension of complication.

Read on for 10 installations from Burning Man 2026 photographed by Chawla.

Cryptomeria by Alexander Rose 

This year's Man Base pavilion was informed by the Jōmon Sugi tree of Japan, which hides its age and gender, a trait that gave the pavilion its cryptic name.

The result was a tree-like platform with a double-helix staircase at its core that allowed festivalgoers to travel up the structure. Recycled wood clad the outside and the structure itself was made from Douglas fir.

"I wanted to use simple materials repeated in organic assemblies to give it a natural feel and create seating nooks among the roots," said Rose.

Temple of the Moon by Moonlight Collective

Led by tech-CEO-turned-artist James Gwertzman, the Moonlight Collective designed the yearly Temple based on the Queen of the Night desert cactus.

From above, the petals of the rare cactus flower can be seen radiating from a central structure made from slats of wood. The core featured a stamen that rose through the top of the structure at its highest point and ended in lights.

Smaller petals were placed around the structure to provide shade and seating. Throughout the week, people hung up memorabilia on the slatted walls of the temple.

On High by Jessy Cusack

Cusack used wood arranged in simple panelling to create "a big, unexpected pulpit" in the desert.

Steel brackets held it together and frosted acrylic gave the doors a glow at night. At the top was a microphone.

"For those who had something they wanted to tell from a mountaintop, we brought the mountain, and then burned it down," said Cussack.

Eiffela Broken Dream by Philippe Maindron

French artist Philippe Maindron transported a large-scale model of the Eiffel Tower to the desert, with the tower broken in half and lying on its side.

The top and bottom of the structure stuck out of the desert at an angle, with lights and a flamethrower attached.

"I chose to fracture the Eiffel Tower in two to explore the tension between collapse and hope," said Maindron. "The lower section evokes the remains of a lost civilisation, while the soaring upper section reaches toward the sky as a symbol of resilience and the possibility of a brighter future."

Apotheneum by Anthony Fieldman & Mark Slee

A "building-scaled multi-sensory visual, sonic, and haptic instrument", Apotheneum was designed with an exterior cube and inner chamber made from string lights.

In total, the installation featured 26,560 lights with integrated sound systems.

The project debuted at Burning Man 2025 before coming back this year, and has since featured at other events, such as Art Basel Miami.

The Gothic Folly by Alex Noerpel and Hunter Keene

This 60-foot-tall structure has the outline of a cathedral complete with stained-glass windows and spires.

Its metal skeleton was fabricated in New York and transported to the desert, where lights were integrated to create an illuminated nighttime display.

Noerpel and Keene said the project was designed to play on "the relationship between weight and presence".

Septima Stella Lux by Dave Ray and Michael Jacob

Glued-laminated timber beams were combined using custom metal joints for this geometric installation on the Playa.

It features four interlocking seven-pointed stars and was designed to be a minimalist approach to the art at Burning Man, according to builder Michael Jacob.

The team is currently seeking a permanent home for the installation.

Chiton Chapel by D'Milo Hallerberg

Engineer and artist D'Milo Hallerberg used 27-foot steel frames to create two facing shells deep in the desert.

The frames were covered with white nylon and the builders included seats around the base. The space, which resembles a mollusc, was used for ceremonies.

The Point Being by Jordan Tenney

This 30-foot-tall timber-framed spire features CNC-carved graphics panels embedded with LEDS.

Steel brackets were used to keep the vertical structure steady in the face of the region's winds.

"Its form deliberately echoes architectural traditions that have long been used to address questions of meaning, transcendence and humanity's place in the cosmos – obelisks, temples and other monumental structures," said Tenney.

Above and Below by Sean Orlando

Orlando worked with Five Ton Crane Arts Collective to suspend a Victorian Cabin 40 feet above the ground on top of a tree-like sculpture.

The fantastical metal tree also had a home at its base with an internal stairway that allowed festivalgoers to climb to the top.

The photography is by Gurpreet Chawla.

item.content:encoded:
Researchers at Parsons School of Design's Healthy Material Lab have released a study that raises concerns about the "many substances harmful to human health" in a typical prefabricated American home.

Called Manufactured Homes: An Analysis of Health and Environmental Impacts of Common Building Materials, the study highlighted potential negative health effects associated with manufactured homes.

Manufactured homes have been popular among Americans for the last century and peaked in the 1970s, with as many as 500,000 delivered per month. That number is now closer to 100,000 per month, according to data from the US Census Bureau.

"Significant health and environmental risks"

"The extensive use of petrochemical-based materials in contemporary manufactured housing poses significant health and environmental risks," said the Healthy Material Lab study.

"Plastics and their associated toxic additives are found in nearly every major surface within a manufactured home, including flooring, paint, cabinetry and insulation."

The fossil-fuel plastics mentioned in the research include polyethylene, polyvinyl chloride and polypropylene, with the majority found in kitchens and bathrooms.

Healthy Material Labs executive design director Jonsara Ruth told Dezeen that the presence of potentially toxic plastic material in homes is a problem across the building industry. However, manufactured homes may pose a greater risk due to the drive for affordability.

Read:

"We need to design for human behaviour if we're ever to get rid of single-use plastics"

"It's true, petroleum-based plastic materials are now widespread in new American homes, not just manufactured ones," said Ruth.

"But manufactured housing offers a unique lens: it's where affordability and conventional construction intersect most starkly, often resulting in material choices that externalize health and environmental costs."

Ruth cited the research of Dr Shanna Swan, who has shown the relationship between plastic exposure and the Green Science Policy Institutes Six Classes framework, which outlines harmful chemicals.

"Longstanding reports, dating back to the 1990s, discuss the increased use of petrochemical-based materials in housing and associated health concerns," said Ruth.

"Famously, the FEMA trailer crisis after Hurricane Katrina highlighted the dangers of high formaldehyde exposure in temporary homes."

The move to healthy affordable homes

The study's results are based on information on materials taken from a single home sold by Northstar Systembuilt in Minnesota, as its sample.

Researchers at Healthy Material Lab called the company, posing as buyers to ask questions about the materials.

"We selected one of the most affordable models from one of the largest manufactured home manufacturers in the US," said Ruth.

"While this isn't a statistically representative sample, it's a typical example of conventional, low-cost manufactured homes."

Read:

Recycled plastics often contain more toxic chemicals says Greenpeace

Ruth said she was confident that the material findings were "consistent with what is often found in affordable, conventional residential construction in the US".

Northstar Systembuilt did not respond to Dezeen's request for comment.

According to Healthy Material Lab, the research's goal was to demonstrate that healthier materials could be used in the construction of these homes. Linoleum flooring could replace vinyl, for example, or wood finishes could be chosen instead of plastic ones.

"We're not arguing against manufactured homes," said Ruth, who added there were some examples of manufacturers trying to improve materials, such as a 2000 collaboration between Enterprise Community Partners and Clayton Homes.

"In fact, we're arguing for healthier, low-carbon prefabricated housing at an affordable price point."

The negative effects of plastic on the body have been examined at length in recent years, especially the ubiquity of microplastics. The National Institute for Health showed the potential for microplastics exposure in the indoor environment, though it did not go so far to claim negative health effects from the exposure.

In 2021, Dezeen took a look at the variety of plastics used in the architecture and design industries.

In 2024, Denmark's Natural Material Studio created a home interior completely free of fossil-fuel-derived products.

item.content:encoded:
Charred-timber cladding is contrasted with warm plywood-lined interiors at House in Mibu, a home in Tochigi Prefecture, Japan, completed by local studio Tato Architects.

The 108-square-metre home was designed for a couple and their three children in the backyard of the client's parental home, tucked off a residential street in the town of Mibu.

As the site needed to accommodate access to an existing garage and workshop, Kobe-based Tato Architects aimed to balance "enclosure and openness" in its design.

According to the studio, this is reflected in the final layout where the first floor overhangs on one side, and the ground floor is sunk 500 millimetres below ground and partially topped with a sloped green roof.

"The core concept is what Dutch architect Aldo van Eyck called the 'in-between' – a realm where enclosure and openness are experienced at once," studio founder Yo Shimada told Dezeen.

"The challenge was to add a whole house without making the yard feel crowded or cutting off the life already flowing through it. Rather than treating these as constraints, we let them shape the building," Shimada continued.

"We sank the living room into the ground and planted its roof with grass: sinking into the earth encloses, touching the earth opens, and the two appear as faces of a single operation."

Read:

Tato Architects uses silver-painted ceilings to draw light into Kyoto home

House in Mibu is entered beneath the overhang of the first floor, where a welcome area with a cloakroom and bathroom steps down into a sunken living, dining and kitchen area.

Full-height windows wrap this lower space to the west, aiming to emphasise its close relationship to the ground while offering views into the neighbouring workshop.

A pair of timber and green-painted steel staircases lead up through a rectilinear void to the home's first floor, where the bedrooms are organised on either side of a raised, loft-like space that can serve as a study or guest room.

The lines of sight created by these stepped levels define the home's interiors, along with walls and ceilings lined entirely in lauan plywood, which Shimada chose for its ability to "record use and age gracefully".

"Sitting in the living room, the ground of the garden spreads out almost at eye level, so family members working in the yard and those inside exchange glances across a slight shift in height," Shimada explained.

"The first floor is the counterpart: a nest-like composition of small rooms – three children's rooms and a bedroom – linked by two staircases, with a loft raised 690 millimetres above the floor that connects the rooms and doubles as a desk or a place to sleep."

Outside, the home is clad in planks of charred cedar and finished with a corrugated metal roof, chosen to nod to the character of the workshop building.

Other homes in Japan recently completed by Tato Architects include a dwelling with similarly open interiors and silver-painted ceilings that help maximise daylight on a compact plot, and a skinny home that is combined with a ceramics studio.

The photography is courtesy of Tato Architects.

Dezeen has announced the interiors shortlist for this year's Dezeen Awards, which includes projects by Isern Serra, Snøhetta and YSG.

The 112 shortlisted projects, which are in the running for awards in 14 different interiors project categories, are by studios located across 26 different countries, including Brazil, Czech Republic, Hong Kong, Kazakhstan, Spain and the United States.

Shortlisted projects include an over-century-old dockside warehouse conversion in Scotland, an apartment defined by chamfered surfaces, warm hues and reinstated art deco features in Australia and an old sailor's home that pays homage to its heritage in Spain.

item.content:encoded:
A lack of money, materials or equipment shaped every object in this mock apartment, which has taken over the basement of London shop Aram as part of an exhibition by guerrilla design collective Design Everything.

With Limitations, which debuted during the London Design Festival, takes the form of an imagined designer's apartment to offer a glimpse behind the curtain at how young creatives are managing to survive in one of the world's most expensive cities.

Every piece in the show was made by one of 102 emerging designers and reflects not just the hurdles they faced in the making process but also the weird, wonderful and ingenious ways they've found to overcome them.

"We hope this will enable you to peek behind the veneer of the design industry – the glossy photographs and Instagram reels – to see an honest portrayal of life as an emerging designer today," Design Everything wrote in the exhibition's introductory text.

In total, the exhibition features 130 objects organised into three distinct rooms – a kitchen, living room and bedroom. And although each was born from different constraints, a lack of funds seemed to be at the root of most limitations faced by young designers.

Stuck for time between her two part-time jobs, designer Symran Shah took to knitting during her commutes as a way of rapid prototyping. Once she was happy with the shape, she sand-cast one of her creations to burn away the cotton yarn and leave behind a deceptively soft-looking metal tray for the bedside table.

Faced with skyrocketing material costs, others resorted to creating new objects from off-the-shelf components, scavenged objects and offcuts.

Among them is a bow-shaped light in the kitchen, made by Design Everything co-founder Lewish Duckworth using an old tent pole and a tensioning guy rope. Nearby, another lamp was assembled from found nitrous oxide canisters by Absolute Beginners, a factory in Park Royal that teaches young people how to make everyday products.

"Funnily enough, NOS canisters came up a lot in the open call," Duckworth laughed.

South London designer Felix Fried lent out his own bed, cobbled together using offcuts from a fabrication job, for the sake of the exhibition and is currently sleeping on a mattress on the floor until the show finishes on 10 October.

Unable to access expensive industrial equipment, others turned to creating improvised production lines in their own homes and hacking their existing machinery.

The speckled backsplash in the apartment's kitchen was made by Royal College of Art student Olivia Webb using wilted flowers from local supermarkets and a DIY tile factory she set up in her flatshare. The everlasting crepe-paper flowers dotted throughout the rest of the kitchen are by criminal defence lawyer-turned-designer Polly Green.

In the absence of a welding machine, Jake Robertson instead made a floor lamp by cutting and bending an aluminium tube "like peeling a banana", and Sam Braid created his Pylon lights from craft wire and masking tape.

"It's almost like a prototype that is so beautiful in its execution, it becomes the final thing," Duckworth said.

Design Everything has made a splash at LDF in recent years by hosting guerrilla shows that offer young and emerging talent a space to exhibit their work for free.

It's a radical departure from existing participation fee models, where even dedicated emerging designer exhibitions, such as Isola, can allegedly charge around £900 per square metre.

"It's very, very inaccessible," explained Design Everything co-founder Tabatha Pearce Chedier, who is exhibiting a series of lights made from wall mouldings.

"I never thought I could show at LDF at all," she admitted.

Read:

Slancha presents Hanging Baskets referencing David Bowie, brutalism and the Romans

Instead of a conventional exhibition, last year's LDF saw Design Everything show 36 chairs by emerging designers from the back of a travelling van. The year before, Duckworth turned the renovation of his friends' record shop into an opportunity to commission work from other young designers he admired.

"The whole point of that show was that you saw the work being used, which became the basis of a lot of what Design Everything is now," he remembered.

"It's about being interactive and playful, about bringing people together, making design feel accessible, and trying to build a community."

This year's show at Aram – a stalwart of the London design scene since 1964 – marks the first time that the collective has gone mainstream.

"They kind of liked our 'punk energy'," Duckworth said.

It's an energy that's very much alive in the Aram show, which doesn't charge a participation fee and encourages visitors to interact with the designs on show instead of placing them on a plinth.

At any given time during the exhibition, Design Everything members, designers and visitors could be found playing with a flat-pack cardboard chess set by Maja Rowecka, perched on sofas made from road signs and bales of cardboard boxes by Charlie Boyden and Max Hayward.

There's also a Jenga set, although this game can't be played since designer Hao Chen has reimagined it as a tiny chest of drawers for holding incense and matchsticks.

In the kitchen, heated conversations about the state of the design industry could be overheard around a dining table assembled from off-the-shelf materials by David Searcy, surrounded by a mishmash of chairs by Jamie Reed, Abby Ghent, Cam Rowley and Gloriana Valverde.

The soundtrack was provided courtesy of a stereo speaker, which designer and DJ David Chen assembled from two £15 IKEA work lamps, 3D-printed adapters and a set of Beyma tweeters.

"I think a lot of us create quite wacky objects," Duckworth said. "And I think being able to engage with them, like actually spend a day with that object, you're like: oh, I actually really like this, and I can see how it would fit within my life."

Throughout the week, the exhibition also hosted live making sessions with some of the designers.

Oliver Linnell assembled a candelabra of nuts and bolts from B&Q's pick-and-mix section, Polly Jennings showed how she slip-casts cups using DIY cardboard moulds, and Anna McAllister used a vegetable steamer and an electric hob to mould balsa wood into a minimalist wall clock, using a process she developed in her own kitchen.

In total, the exhibition features 130 objects by 102 designers, which might sound like a lot but is only a fraction of the 520 submissions that Design Everything received to its open call – more than three times as many as last year.

"I hope it's because we feel accessible that people apply with stuff that they've made and feel like there's an opportunity there instead of being intimidated and put off," Duckworth said.

The Design Everything team – Jacob Marks, Eleanor Murphy, Sammi Cherryman, Izi Thexton, Duckworth and Pearce Chedier, with him from Sandro Hernandez Rosales – went through each project and developed a points system to rank them based on how well they fit the theme and what was needed for the apartment.

The team also spoke to each of the 102 participants about the limitations they face and photographed some of the spaces they work out of, with the results collated in the final part of the exhibition.

In total, the process of organising the exhibition took around six months, during which the members also created their own contributions to the show and held down their day jobs.

"Everyone's kind of got their bread and butter," Duckworth explained. "It's a bit of a passion project for now. But we're hoping that we can get some funding soon."

The photography is by Kane Hulse.

With Limitations is on show from 11 September to 10 October 2026 as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen Showroom: Portuguese brand GenCork combines one of the world's most sustainable natural materials with customisable algorithmically generated design, creating an insulating wall cladding that makes a strong visual impression.

GenCork's CorkVector Panel is made using the Corkvectors algorithm – created by creative director and designer Le Brimet – which blends organic patterns inspired by nature with geometric structure to create a dynamic 3D surface design.

The panels make use of cork, which is a highly renewable material, harvested from trees without cutting them down and so allowing forests to continually regenerate.

GenCork's owner and producer Sofalca lowers the environmental impact even further with its expanded black cork, which is made using a zero-waste process where steam from waste biomass from the cork's cleaning and milling bonds the material together with only its natural resin.

This process also gives the panels their distinctive rich colour, darker and earthier than raw cork, while CNC milling gives it its precise relief.

The computational design system allows the pattern to be customised to the dimensions of the wall or other parameters, while cork's strong thermal and acoustic insulating properties make the product as functional as it is aesthetic.

"Corkvectors [is] a bridge between nature and design, evoking the beauty of both," said GenCork.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Grimshaw has designed three stations for City Rail Link in Auckland, New Zealand, guided by Māori cultural values that aim to connect the buildings to their sites.

The three city-centre stations, named Te Waihorotiu, Karanga-a-Hape and Maungawhau, form part of development of the City Rail Link, which will double the city's existing rail network capacity.

According to Grimshaw, the expansion is the "largest transport infrastructure project ever undertaken in New Zealand".

It was developed in partnership with Mana Whenua, the Māori group that has customary authority over the land, and guided by the Te Aranga Māori Design Principles aligned with Māori cultural values.

Grimshaw developed a series of architectural elements with various layers of dark, light and translucent materiality applied across all three stations to express Te Whaiao – the creation story of Māori narrative representing the first glimmer of dawn.

According to the studio, it developed four architectural elements – Sky, Earth, Threshold and Fourth – to interpret the narrative into the station design.

Each station is clad with aluminium screens on the facade of the air-handling plant room. Using parametric design tools, Grimshaw created a distinct pattern for each station by assembling twelve shingle types combined with fixing rails.

The patterns on the facade connect to traditional Māori artwork that express the qualities of the sky.

Local geology was reflected through the material choice of the flooring, responding to the Earth element.

Modular precast panels were used at Te Waihorotiu and Karanga-a-Hape stations, while Maungawhau Station uses sandstone and basalt floors.

In an effort to create a unique narrative for each station, site-specific artworks nominated by Mana Whenua were placed in the entrance halls of each building.

These artworks were built into the fabric of the buildings to make them integral to the stations, rather than applied as a separate layer.

At Te Waihorotiu, artist Graham Tipene created Horotiu, a ceiling installation within the foyer at the Wellesley Street entrance.

It comprises over 4,000 golden anodised aluminium rods, evoking the movement of bulrush reeds growing in the local Waihorotiu Stream.

A kauri wood carving crafted by Paraone Luiten-Apirana was positioned at the centre of the installation.

It takes the form of a sea-serpent called Horotiu, known as the guardian of the area.

Read:

Grimshaw to integrate Boring Company station into elevated Las Vegas stadium plaza

Within the Mercury Lane entrance at Karanga-a-Hape Station, Reuben Kirkwood created three snail-shell sculptures using anodised aluminium radiating panels, symbolising connection between people and nature.

At the same station, Kirkwood created a ceiling artwork within the Beresford Street entrance that aims to showcase the relationship between the power of the sun and the phases of the moon and tides, which is the form of the traditional Māori lunar calendar.

Artist Tessa Harris designed triangular forms crafted by Sofia Athineou for the Maungawhau Station, to reference the volcanic mountain it was named after.

The studio aimed to create a design language for the stations, with consistent wall-lining and batten ceilings used across the stations.

"This is infrastructure that will change forever how Auckland moves," said Grimshaw group managing partner Mark Middleton.

"Its enduring value lies in the relationship between transport, public space and cultural identity – a network designed for Tāmaki Makaurau and the generations who will use it."

Elsewhere, the studio recently released plans for a reimagined entry plaza for Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas.
