item.content:encoded:
Local studio I IN drew on the existing architecture when creating fashion brand Andersson Bell's flagship store in Japan, which is filled with glossy, reflective surfaces and warm red and yellow hues.

Located in Tokyo's Aoyama neighbourhood, the original building from 1993 has an exposed concrete interior that heavily influenced I IN's design for the store.

"It is quite rare to find such a magnificent space in Tokyo, and we were fortunate to have the freedom to take a bold and radical approach to the design," I IN co-founder Yohei Terui told Dezeen.

"Especially, the building's strong composition of mass and void became a major source of inspiration and guided us throughout the spatial planning."

The studio aimed for the interior to be contrasting but not competing with the architecture.

"The idea was to translate the brand's identity of 'contrast' into space design," Terui continued.

"The existing architecture, built in Tokyo in the 90s, already had a very strong character and presence, so rather than competing with it, we wanted to introduce a strong modern layer that would create a beautiful contrast with the existing architecture."

To do so, I IN, which Terui founded with Hiromu Yuyama, introduced warm, saturated colours across the building's three storeys.

Bright red, orange and yellow hues contrast against the boardmarked concrete walls throughout the space, with the red section also visible through the store's large front window.

"The red comes from the brand's signature colour and became the introduction of the store," Terui said.

"As guests move through the space and step upstairs, they experience a gradual transition from red to orange and then to yellow," he continued.

"Rather than simply applying colour to each floor, we wanted this transition to become part of the spatial experience, giving each level a different atmosphere and creating a sense of progression as guests move through the building."

Read:

I IN uses glossy surfaces and Edo purple to create "new form of Japanese luxury" for Ginza Lounge

Terui and Yuyama also added pipes that "extend through the existing architecture as if piercing its structure", the studio said.

As well as contrasting the concrete's grey hue with more colourful details, I IN juxtaposed its raw tactility with plenty of glossy and mirrored details, including a glass floor, steel pipes and tables and display cases with shiny, lacquered surfaces.

The furniture pieces used in the 309-square-metre store were tailor-made by the studio and designed to feel like a part of the existing architecture.

"All of the furniture was custom-made for the store," Terui said.

"We followed the same idea of creating a bold presence, taking inspiration from the powerful character and scale of the existing architecture," he continued.

"Rather than treating the furniture as separate elements placed within the space, we designed each piece as a part of the architecture, as if it had always been there, so that the furniture and the space ultimately merge into one."

I IN has previously also designed a tile-clad store for designer Nigo's Human Made brand and a glossy purple lounge for department store Matsuya Ginza.

The photography is by Tomooki Kengaku.

item.content:encoded:
London-based designer Billy Easter has released a cubic table lamp made from silicone that can change colour by manually slotting different translucent slabs into it.

The Gel Lamp, released last month through Easter's studio Public Parts, comprises a hollow cube of silicone –measuring approximately 11.5-by-11.5-by-11.5 centimetres – the base of which contains a dimmable LED.

A slim slot sits towards the bottom of the lamp's body, into which slices of transparent coloured gels, also made of silicone, can be slid, changing the colour of the light accordingly.

Easter was informed by the thin films of coloured gel used in photography, studio and theatre lighting, which are placed directly over the lens to change the colour of light.

The designer created 3D-printed moulds into which she prepared and poured liquid silicone. Curing and casting each side of the lamp takes a matter of days, after which the lamps are hand-finished. The same process applies to the coloured slides.

The light source itself is held within a recessed void rather than being permanently embedded within the silicone, making the electronics easy to access and replace when needed and extending the lamp's lifetime.

Easter created 13 coloured slabs – all featuring the studio's name embossed along one edge – that transform the light from its default cool white to a rainbow of different hues.

"There's a small sense of ritual to the Gel Lamp," Easter told Dezeen. "I like the physical act of choosing a colour and sliding the gel into the lamp to change the atmosphere of a room."

"It's a very simple interaction, but it makes adjusting the light feel more tactile and deliberate than pressing a button or changing a setting on a screen," she continued.

Despite its capacity for changing colour, the designer also envisages the lamp being a design object in its own right even when not lit up.

"It's important to me that the lamps have a presence as sculptural objects when they're switched off," Easter said.

Read:

Brecht Wright Gander's Flesh Light lamp sheds light on "mechanical servants"

Despite the lamps' statuesque appearance, the silicone material makes them surprisingly durable and readily cleanable, allowing them to withstand the day-to-day knocks and bumps of domestic life.

As well as residential spaces, the designer envisages them being used in hospitality interiors to provide warmth, intimacy and visual interest.

The lamp is produced in individually-numbered batches of limited amounts. The lamp's cost of £375 includes a single lamp as well as two interchangeable silicone gel slabs.

Easter specialises in the design and manufacturing of hand-cast silicone objects. Alongside the Gel Lamp, previous releases have included silicone coasters, wearables and sex toys.

Other lamp designs recently published on Dezeen include Ilse Crawford's understated lamps for IKEA, a lamp by Blond designed by a 12-year-old and statuesque lamps made from surplus glassware.

item.content:encoded:
US studio MOS Architects has used aluminium shingles to cover an egg-shaped pavilion at Art Omi in Upstate New York, creating a place to rest that draws stylistically on pre-modern basketry and mid-century futurism.

An experiment in form and material, A Dome with Four Oculi was installed on the expansive Art Omi campus as a place of shelter and rest.

The structure sits on stilts and consists of a shell that MOS compared to a crinoline dress.

It was then covered by aluminium shingles that overlap and are held in place by stainless steel bolts. Combined, the shell is around a quarter-inch thick. It has two portholes on the side that look out into the landscape and is open at the top.

MOS co-founder Michael Meredith told Dezeen that structurally it is like an "upside-down basket", connecting to both the studio's work in easy-to-assemble prefabricated aluminium structures and a focus on the potential for experimentation at small scales.

"We've been working for years with folded aluminium and basically using it like paper, almost like large-scale models," said Meredith.

It was designed to be put together with standard tools in just a few days.

Conceptually, the structure takes cues both from pre-modern basketry as well as from the Airstream trailer.

"There's something of woven architecture in it, almost pre-modern," said Meredith. "Woven structures have an economic use of material, lighter material in this case. There's something nomadic."

"But there's Airstream trailer quality too," he continued. "You can see a bunch of stuff in it."

Beyond the thematic elements, the structure also provides shelter and a place to sit in the fields of Art Omi, which hold dozens of rotating art and architecture installations.

The oculi on the sides of the structure also provide vistas across the field.

Triangular cutouts on the side provide access and give the structure as in a tent.

Viewed from elsewhere, the pavilion has a face-like quality. It almost looks like the top part of the head of the Iron Giant from the 1999 film.

"It's also, as everybody tells us, a little bit ridiculous," said Meredith, who said it was like a Buckminster Fuller dome reimagined by artist Philip Guston. He added that the woven nature of these structures makes it more practical than typical domes, as the sides could be modified and shaped as in basketry.

Read:

Studio Maks tops science pavilion in Austria with undulating mirrored roof

MOS is well known for its conceptual work and writings.

A Dome with Four Oculi relates to recent writings by the studio, such as its Smaller Architecture book, which calls for smaller architecture studios to experiment.

It was developed partly in response to what Meredith calls a "weird moment" for architecture. The prevalence and desire for bigness have left out an important space that architecture holds for expression.

"Architecture is in a weird moment in general. It used to be a more active part of cultural production," he said.

"At some point, though, it sort of shifted and just feels commercial. Everything just feels like a commodity," he continued.

"So that's what's nice about Art Omi. It's sort of outside the system, and it gives you a chance to reflect and think about something else."

The pavilion was part of Art Omi's fall architecture programming, which included TAELON7's Limbo Engawa pavilion.

Art Omi has been doubling down on its commitment to architecture and, in 2024, announced a series of 18 pavilions designed by established architecture studios such as SO-IL.

In London, Studio Saar created a shield-topped pavilion for London Design Festival, examining Britain's colonial history in India.

The photography is by Michael Vahrenwald.

item.content:encoded:
New York City plans to relocate inmates from Rikers Island into four jails built from the ground up in Queens, Brooklyn, Manhattan and the Bronx. Here, Dezeen looks at the architecture of each project.

Begun in 2017, the NYC Borough-Based Jail Program (BBJ) is largely overseen by the New York City Department of Design and Construction (DDC), which is working with a variety of architecture studios on each jail, including HOK, Cetra Ruddy and Michael Graves.

With the recent groundbreaking of the Manhattan jail, construction of all four borough-based jails has begun, while the city simultaneously makes steps towards closing the Rikers Island jail complex.

The Brooklyn jail, which is the furthest along, is set to open in 2029. The other three jails are expected to be completed in the early 2030s.

Read:

"Stop working on spaces which disproportionately impact African Americans" says architectural designer Michael Ford

Justice design is a contested field within architecture. Some believe that architects should not be working in this sector at all. In 2020, the AIA New York issued a statement urging studios to "move away" from the design of prisons, jails and other detention centres.

However, others believe that good architecture can better serve the incarcerated population.

HOK, which has designed two of the four BBJ jails and has a dedicated justice design arm, said it does not "shy away" from the projects.

"We think it's our responsibility as architects to help solve some serious social problems, and we don't shy away from them," HOK New York design principal Ken Drucker told Dezeen.

Read:

"New York's new prisons will be more than just places of incarceration"

The DDC has a list of design goals for the program, including mental health programming for those in custody, safe environments for staff, visitors and inmates, and "good civic architecture" that relates to its surrounding neighbourhood.

In design documents, cells have horizontally barred windows, a single bed, a desk underneath the window, a stool and a toilet. For the Manhattan project, HOK is integrating circadian-rhythm lighting synced to the outdoors to replace harsh overhead lighting found in older facilities.

In some cells, inmates have access to a reading light they can control.

"This design strategy is really meant to be something that the people can thrive in, and it's not just a place where they always feel like they're on the defence all the time," said HOK director of civic + justice Jeff Goodale. 

The DDC and studios are also working to create "welcoming" interior visiting centres, as the projects purport a strong focus on providing dignified spaces not only for those incarcerated, but for visitors and staff.

Interior renders show open waiting rooms clad in "warm" materials, with an emphasis on clear, direct circulation through the space. Spaces for contact and no-contact visitations and children's play areas with bright carpeting and bookshelves are also present in the designs.

Local communities have opposed the projects. Some have held rallies and protests during the past several years as construction moves forward. Some of the projects, such as the Queens facility, are still making design adjustments.

More recently, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani called Rikers Island one of the "deepest failures of our city government" and said the city is "replacing a system built around neglect with one centred on rehabilitation".

Read on for a closer look at these facilities.

Manhattan Detention Facility, Chinatown, by HOK

Located at 125 White Street in Chinatown, the Manhattan Detention Facility will be the tallest jail in the world when completed.

The design is broken into "four vertical quadrants", with a large, 55-foot-tall (16 metres tall) pedestrian passageway underneath the building. The passageway was meant to integrate the building with its surrounding site at the nexus of Chinatown, Little Italy, Tribeca and the civic district to the south, according to HOK.

The jail, which will replace a former detention centre on the same site, has brought pushback and engagement from the local community, with the DDC and HOK noting the neighbourhood has been "very vocal" in the design process.

Site preparation is underway, but not without concerns about feasibility from local leaders, who recently penned a letter to mayor Mamdani asking for a reassessment of the site.

Find out more about the Manhattan Detention Facility ›

Brooklyn Borough-Based Jail, Boerum Hill, by HOK

Located at 275 Atlantic Avenue on the site of a former jail, the Brooklyn Borough-Based Jail is the nearest to completion. It towers above the low-rise neighbourhoods to the south.

According to HOK, its design focused primarily on bringing daylight to occupants and as deep into the building as possible, with each cell connected directly to an outdoor space completely surrounded by expanded metal security mesh.

"One of the things that we've seen in facilities where people have to be escorted to a central place for outdoor space is that often they don't get there, and with putting the outdoor space directly attached to the living unit, people will be out there daily," said Goodale.

The studio clad the building in fixed fins to control daylighting angles, and terracotta to reflect materials found in the neighbourhood.

Bronx Borough-Based Jail Facility, Mott Haven, by CetraRuddy, Lumen Architects and Urbahn Architects

The 11-storey Bronx Borough-Based Jail Facility is located on the site of a former hospital and New York City Police impound lot.

The facility will contain 40,000 square feet (3,716 square meters) of community and commercial space on the ground floor, dedicated space for on-site services and programming, indoor and outdoor recreation, food services, staff offices and facilities, according to the DDC. It will also contain spaces such as areas for children and nursing mothers.

In the final community design meeting in March 2026, Urbahn Architects associate principal Larry Gutterman explained the building's three-storey podium lines up with the height of nearby residential rowhouses. According to the studio, the mesh-clad tower relates to the scale of surrounding industrial buildings.

A major concern from the community, according to the team, was the scale of the building, which the studio attempted to mitigate by creating several stepped volumes.

Find out more about Bronx Borough-Based Jail Facility ›

Queens Borough-Based Jail Facility, Kew Gardens, by STV and Michael Graves

The Queens Borough-Based Jail Facility is located at 126-02 82nd Avenue, on the same site as the current Queens Detention Center and a large parking lot. It is the only BBJ that includes beds for women and "gender expansive" inmates, according to the DDC. Spaces such as a nursery and a women's "law library" are shown in the design.

The site contains three individual "housing towers" clad in metal mesh around its recreation areas, precast concrete around its base, and metal panels and glass curtain walls on the upper floors.

A smaller parking garage building with a community space was completed in June 2023 as part of the project, which sits off to the side.

In the most recent design meeting, the team said it's working on updates such as replacing natural wood cladding with more durable materials and making the project overall more ADA accessible.

item.content:encoded:
UK studio RX Architects has returned to a house it previously completed in Sussex to add an extension, designed to blend in with the existing timber-clad form.

The original home, named Druim, was completed in 2020 on the Rye Nature Reserve in East Sussex. The project involved altering a half-built structure that had been sold with the site.

While the original project focused on views of the nature reserve and sea, RX Architects looked to improve the home's connection to the more private rear garden with the Druim Extension.

"The main opportunity was to enhance the private rear gardens and connections to the northern aspect to the outside space," studio director Rob Pollard told Dezeen.

"The original design didn't allow this, due to budget limitations at that time, making it more complex to adapt the originally built structure," he explained.

"We wanted the new adaptations to tie in seamlessly with the original house, as we had only completed the original property seven years ago or so. Therefore, we used the same contractor and materials on the scheme."

Druim Extension houses an expanded dining area, which is wrapped by full-height glazing and sliding doors that open onto a patio and the home's garden.

This space, which connects to the existing kitchen to the east, has been organised around a solid wood table, large skylight and log burner at its centre.

Tucked into the glazed, garden-facing corner of this dining space is a large window seat, shaded by deep soffits clad in narrow timber planks that continue inside to define the extension's ceilings.

"The rear extension provides a break and depth to the rear elevation which sits neatly into the landscape – but internally it creates a genuine sense of being outdoors and immersed in the garden, which the original property didn't have," Pollard explained.

"The clad ceiling, overhanging soffits, glazed elevations and corner window seat have a real sense of calm, as they are completely sheltered from the southern aspect, which is more exposed to the harsh winds from the coast," he added.

Read:

Loader Monteith rebuilds ruined Highlands house with blackened-larch extension

As well as expanding the interior, Druim Extension also prompted a reorientation of the existing spaces around a new boot room and entrance hall, providing direct access to the staircase, which was previously accessed from the living room.

To the west of the entrance, a glazed linking corridor replaces a paved path leading to the home's annexe, helping to shelter the home's garden from coastal winds while still allowing views through.

"Turning the stair allowed the living room orientation to shift, providing a better aspect for views out to the sea and nature reserve," Pollard said.

"The glazed link gives the whole building more of a horizontal emphasis, but also provides a fantastic rear courtyard to the garden, which gives views through it to the sea and nature reserve."

Elsewhere in Sussex, DeDraft recently updated a modernist home set within a garden, using a palette of warm wood and ceramic tiles to echo the original design.

Other projects by RX Architects include Seabreeze, a coastal home in East Sussex that was finished in pale pink-toned concrete to evoke Mediterranean beach houses.

The photography is by Richard Chivers.

item.content:encoded:
The University of the Arts London has transformed a drab guest quarters at one of its colleges into a colourful showcase that lets visitors eat, sleep and bathe in student and graduate design.

The two-bedroom Atterbury Flat – located on the Chelsea College of Arts campus, a Grade II listed former Royal Army Medical College building – has been used to host visiting professors and dignitaries since the university moved into the premises in 2005.

But University of the Arts (UAL) lecturer Zoë Tynan-Campbell saw an opportunity to turn it into something more – a living and "live-in" archive of student work that had so far gone largely uncollected by the university.

UAL is the second top-ranked university for art and design in the world, with six colleges including Central Saint Martins under its banner, allowing her to draw from a deep well of talent.

Working with alumni Abigail Rigby and Bhairavi Yogasivam as co-curators, Tynan-Campbell engaged more than 400 students and graduates from 58 courses across all colleges in the endeavour, ultimately purchasing 117 works for the first round of acquisitions.

These range from fantastical pieces that attracted attention at graduate shows – like a colour-changing chair and a conceptual coffee table made of 160 kilograms of stacked paper – to widely available products from companies established by UAL veterans.

The latter category includes refillable soap by Blackmarket, foldable clothes hangers by Easy Hang and cookware hand-moulded from Indian river clay by Tiipoi.

Many of the pieces were made specifically for the flat, including bathroom tiles and a matching sink in a gradient of greens by ceramicist and County Hall Pottery director Emma Louise Payne, as well as a giant pencil by multidisciplinary designer Neha Ratanchand for signing the guestbook.

No object is too small to be unworthy of creative attention – a pair of scissors, a pack of tarot cards, several tea towels and a recycling bag made of recycled bags are among the alumni contributions – but some ordinary furniture from the old flat remains, awaiting replacement as the archive expands.

"Part of the intention is asking questions around what we collect and what we value," said Tynan-Campbell. "Because we have a fine art collection as an institution... but most of it is paintings and photographs and 2D work, basically."

"So this is us saying, okay, well, we have six universities, we have so many different disciplines, why is only fine art worth collecting?" she continued. "Why are we not collecting the narratives, the stories, the objects that all these other courses are producing?"

"And of course, there's loads of practical reasons why not. One is space, which is why this is perfect, because we didn't have to build a space. This was here, and it was a blank canvas."

Read:

Pangolin seating changes colour like a mood ring in response to touch

The Atterbury Flat was unveiled last week at the London Design Festival and will continue serving as a temporary home for visiting professors and other guests now that the event is over.

Dezeen had the pleasure of a night's stay during the festival and can report that the mismatched wooden door handles by product design student Nora Hinsch function, the precisely honed mugs by architect-turned-ceramicist John Robertson are perfect to cradle, and the softly psychedelic 3D-printed botanical bedside lamps by Yichun Lu are soothing to watch alone in the dark.

Tynan-Campbell sees the takeover of the Atterbury Flat as a new model for commissioning and archiving student work. As far as she is aware, it is the first archive of this type, doubling as a residence at a university.

The project saw £61,686 paid directly to students and grads for their work – 91.98 per cent of the total budget.

In addition to selecting the pieces and shepherding new commissions to completion, Tynan-Campbell and her co-curators took charge of the interior and spatial design, using a colour palette adapted from a work by Molly Cook as a jumping-off point.

Tynan-Campbell had discovered Cook in the first room at the first degree show she scouted, where the multidisciplinary designer presented a project that involved the careful study of a location through photography, drawing and listening to arrive at its idiosyncratic colour palette.

The graphic print she made using the same methodology for the Atterbury Flat hangs in the kitchen and was provided as a reference to the other participants.

"We set out [on this project] saying, this is an act of radical trust in what your students can do," said Tynan-Campbell. "Give them the opportunity, not an external agency or firm. I feel like literally every one of them really rose to the occasion."

The Atterbury Flat was on show from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen has announced the architecture shortlist for this year's Dezeen Awards, which includes buildings by Dorte Mandrup, Farshid Moussavi Architects and Herzog & de Meuron.

The 152 shortlisted projects, which are in the running for awards in 19 different architecture project categories, are by studios located across 36 different countries, including China, Finland, Kuwait, Portugal, Thailand and Uruguay.

Shortlisted projects include a country house with walls formed of unstabilised rammed earth in the UK, a trio of squat guesthouses characterised by glass walls and thatched roofs in Ukraine and a mosque with a perforated, blanket-like roof of stone-clad steelwork in Qatar.

The shortlist also features an office that reimagines machiya housing with "breathing" metal awnings in Japan and a sprawling brick-clad university building modelled on stepped wells in India.

Dezeen Awards 2026 shortlists revealed this week

Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble, will reveal all shortlisted projects this week. The interiors shortlist will be published tomorrow, followed by the design shortlist on Wednesday.

item.title: Trump triumphal arch to become "top grade military complex" for launching drones
item.dc:creator: Tom Ravenscroft

item.content:encoded:
US president Donald Trump has announced that the planned 250-foot-high triumphal arch in Washington DC, designed by Atlanta-based Harrison Design, will now be a military base with drones and snipers.

According to Trump, who announced the plan in a Truth Social post yesterday, the change in the design was made at the request of the US military.

"At the strong request of the United States military, and for national security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent triumphal arch... into a top grade military complex/triumphal arch," he said.

Set to be built alongside the Arlington Memorial Bridge on the south bank of the Potomac River, the neoclassical arch is planned to be 250 feet high (76 metres) – nearly 100 feet (30 metres) higher than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.

Plans for the arch were first revealed last October, with US interior secretary Doug Burgum announcing that construct was about to begin earlier this month.

The plans gained approval from the Commission of Fine Arts in May and the National Capital Planning Commission in July.

According to Trump, the arch will now be used for the storage and deployment of "large numbers of drones", as well as a base for sniper units with "large quantities" of ammunition.

"[It will] house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage," he said.

Read:

US Supreme Court says construction of Trump's White House ballroom can continue

Previously, the arch was planned as a tourist attraction topped with a publicly accessible viewpoint. Plans of the arch showed its interior spaces housing facilities for visitors, including galleries for exhibitions.

It is unclear how these spaces will be impacted by the plans to use the structure for military purposes, or how the plans will impact the arch's planning approvals.

Trump's decision to tie the construction of the monument to national security follows a similar move at the White House, where a ballroom is being built onto an extensive, underground military complex.

Recently, the US Supreme Court ruled that construction can continue on the ballroom despite numerous attempts to halt progress on the building.

item.content:encoded:
Fashion brand Homme Plissé Issey Miyake has created a capsule collection for London's Tate Modern art gallery, which was informed by Henri Matisse's artwork The Snail and revealed as part of a dance performance.

The Japanese brand showed the collection in one of its Open Studio events, a global initiative by Issey Miyake to present its clothes in places where they haven't been seen before.

The Tate performance was its second edition and saw Homme Plissé Issey Miyake present a capsule collection informed by one of the gallery's artworks, The Snail by Henry Matisse.

The collage of vibrant, colourful pieces of paper formed the base of the clothing line, which was unveiled in a performance by the Dresden Frankfurt Dance Company last week on a set by Studio Dennis Vanderbroeck.

Located in Tate Modern's The Tanks – its permanent galleries for live art – the performance saw dancers move over a felt-covered floor, with benches and seats arranged around the circular concrete walls of the room.

As part of the performance, they lifted cut-outs from the floor to reveal the colourful garments in the brand's signature pleated designs, which they then wore as they continued to dance.

For the final part of the performance, the dancers lifted a large section of the floor to reveal a fabric version of The Snail artwork underneath, while wearing designs from the capsule collection decorated with the collage.

The brand chose London for the second Open Studio edition as it felt that Tate's work with designers made it a suitable partner.

Read:

SO–IL completes "clean, precise, audacious" Issey Miyake store in New York

"We decided to do the second edition of Open Studio in London because, through a common referral, we got a proposal from Tate," Satoshi Kondo, a member of the Homme Plissé Issey Miyake design team, told Dezeen.

"Being aware of Tate's engagement in working with designers to design something based on their permanent collection, we found a synergy between the offer and what Open Studio is."

Kondo, who is also the artistic director of the Issey Miyake mainline, said he is a big fan of Tate Modern and always visits it when he is in London.

"What Tate represents is this approach that art is open to everyone, so it's accessible to any person," Kondo said.

"Part of the Tate's permanent collection is open to the public for free, so whenever you come in, there are people making drawings and families spending time here."

This ethos ties in with what Issey Miyake wants to do with its Open Studio events, Kondo explained.

"The environment and the institution itself is quite liberal and open to the public, and that also really speaks to the intention of Open Studio – it's to open up and to really share with the local communities, in this case London, how we design and how we make clothing," he concluded.

The capsule collection will be on sale at Tate Modern before becoming globally available early next year.

Issey Miyake also recently unveiled its new flagship store in New York, designed by SO-IL, and showcased handcrafted paper furniture during this year's Milan design week.

Dezeen Showroom: surfaces brand VitrA Tiles celebrates the beauty of several of the world's natural stones with its Geocode collection of wall and floor tiles.

The Geocode collection combines the calming beauty of natural colours and textures with the performance qualities suited to everyday living.

Its surfaces feature expressive veining and textural depth created through VitrA Tiles' advanced surface technologies, giving an effect that is both realistic and alluring.

The designs in the collection include Alba, based on historic Piedra de Campaspero limestone, and Imperio, inspired by the marble of the Taj Mahal.

Rio brings the marble-like mineral movement of Brazilian Quarzite, while Merano emulates the cool depths of Italian Gneiss.

The Geocode tiles are part of VitrA Tiles' Code series, transforming natural references into high-performance ceramic surfaces that meet the needs of contemporary architecture and interior design.

item.content:encoded:
Lazy attempts to frame interiors products as more inclusive for neurodivergent people are becoming too common, writes Ellie Foster.

Most of us would agree that increasing awareness around neurodiversity is important and overdue, with 15-20 per cent of the global population demonstrating traits of ADHD, autism, dyslexia and the like. It makes sense that interior designers pursuing a more inclusively built world are following the conversation closely, asking themselves to better accommodate those who interpret and experience space differently.

For better or worse, product manufacturers have been following along too. However, too often, neurodiverse design is merely a marketing ploy.

Is neurodiverse design just another gap in the market to exploit, similar to greenwashing before it?

Naturally, some contract furnishers will bristle at that accusation, and for specifiers aiming to envelope people up and down the spectrum it may also rankle. But recent industry events and product launches make it difficult for me to come to any other conclusion.

In the past three years, there has been no shortage of events championing "designing for difference" in my inbox; no lack of press releases pulling on the terms hypo- and hypersensitivity to explain that a task chair comes in both brights and neutrals.

More recently, the sheer volume of these kinds of emails has raised questions for me about honest intentions. Do this many manufacturers really care about making products that improve the wellbeing of all?

Read:

"Many of our everyday spaces are doing us harm"

Or, is neurodiverse design just another gap in the market to exploit, similar to greenwashing before it? Having a heightened awareness of space myself, these are the same questions that have started to gnaw at my conscience in a big way.

For more than a few brands, the plan of attack has been to showcase how updated furniture collections soothe individuals overstimulated by clashing patterns and loud colours, and energise those rendered lethargic by muted tones and minimalism.

At last year's Clerkenwell Design Week, one commercial name hosted a showroom installation addressing the acute sensory needs associated with certain diagnoses. Once attendees had marvelled at the work, the structure doubled as a backdrop for a talks programme on how we can be kinder to neurodivergent employees and service users through the use of design.

The focus on colour overlooks the psychological and physiological impact that objects have on neurodiverse brains

The activation then linked to a new luxury vinyl tile collection – one that looked similar to the brand's previous lines, but professed to ease mental anguish nonetheless.

All that is to say, the event was good; well-intentioned, well-received. The tenuously linked PVC planks in Herringbone, Chevron and Checkerboard? Not so much.

The fanfare around ever-so-slightly tweaked product ranges rarely ventures beyond those two "H" words (hyposensitivity and hypersensitivity), which are almost exclusively used in the context of colour. The main outcome – for me, at least – is a subtle repositioning of said brand as the ethical choice, alongside an excuse to mass produce its current portfolio in a range of new and "progressive" hues.

Read:

First autistic Barbie allows "more children to see themselves" in doll

The focus on colour overlooks the psychological and physiological impact that objects have on neurodiverse brains in other ways. Low-hanging light fixtures leading to feelings of claustrophobia; castor-mounted furniture causing emotional instability; chairs with too many components creating distraction or obsessive compulsions.

These are just a few topics that could broaden the conversation around neurodiversity in product design – and the fact that we're still accepting that additional Cobalt and Stone colourways are enough to prevent meltdowns only proves that the area remains chronically understudied.

I want to urge interior designers not to take things at face value

From where I'm sitting (and that's in a central Manchester co-working space revamped just a year ago), it seems obvious that often it's just a rebranding of the same old products. Neurodiverse-friendly lounge chairs come in the same kaleidoscopic fabrics that were once flogged in the name of "design versatility"; those with stripped-back aesthetics – at one time marketed to fans of wabi-sabi or biophilic design trends – are now prime for people overwhelmed by pattern complexity and vibrance.

Repackaging collections that already exist shows a significant lack of care for people whose entire worldview can be skewed by spatial discordance, as manufacturers continue to cash in on industry-wide conversations around diverse perspectives.

Read:

"Space that is exclusionary does not live up to its full potential"

I want to urge interior designers not to take things at face value. To read between the lines on brands pushing a "designing for difference" rhetoric, to uncover whether these same brands championed neurodiversity before it became a global talking point.

It's also worth investigating whether neurodiverse individuals have been involved in the product design process at all or if, at the very least, the process was informed by talking to them directly.

It goes without saying that product and interior designers mutually aspiring for more inclusive interior settings is a positive thing, but the problem lies in the recent surge of stuff that overpromises and under-delivers. The risk is that marketing products in this way leaves neurodiverse occupants failed, and designers mis-sold.

Ellie Foster is an architecture and design journalist based in Manchester.

item.content:encoded:
Projects using reclaimed natural materials and local resources proved popular at this year's Oslo Architecture Triennale. From innovative wool tiles to monolithic stone walls, we round up key highlights from the event.

In its ninth edition, this year's Oslo Architecture Triennale includes exhibitions, seminars and workshops centred around the theme What If Nature Comes First?

Taking place from 17 September to 1 October at Oslo's Sofienberg Church, many of the projects on display in the main exhibition championed the reuse of various natural materials and sourcing materials locally.

"This triennale shows what architecture looks like when nature comes first"

"Construction is one of the biggest single drivers of nature loss and emissions, and we keep building and demolishing the way we always have," said Oslo Architecture Triennale director Line Ramstad.

"What we talk about too little is how much is already available to us in materials, in buildings that still stand, and in knowledge we already have," she continued.

"This triennale shows what architecture looks like when nature comes first, and what it would take to scale solutions that already exist."

Read on for five stand-out projects at the Oslo Architecture Triennale:

Upcycling Wool Ecologies by Grinham Research Group

An installation cloaked in multicoloured fluted tiles made from waste sheep wool was presented at the triennale by the Grinham Research Group at Harvard University.

To make the tiles, wool is treated with an alkaline solution that partially breaks down its keratin proteins into a gel, which is then crosslinked and combined with residual wool fibres to form a petrochemical-free plastic material.

Conceptualised for retrofitting the outside of buildings, the tiles have a multi-layer design made up of a low-density back panel that acts as an insulative board and a denser outer panel with a fluted surface that is more durable and weatherised.

"We're looking at this application because external retrofits are less cost-prohibitive – replacing interior insulation is more cost-prohibitive because you need to dig into the wall," said Harvard University researcher Leonard Palmer.

"There is an abundance of waste wool in the world," he continued. "Sheep wool is like nature's plastic; it has really good properties – it's insulative, fire-resistant and anti-bacterial."

Lasting Larvikite by Martin Hopland and Studio Wideroe

Oslo-based architecture firms Arkitekt Martin Hopland and architecture firm Studio Wideroe collaborated on a trio of stone wall prototypes, which they assembled using Larvikite stone from Norway's Larvik quarry.

One wall has a mismatched mosaic appearance made entirely from excess stone, another features a profile pattern of horizontal bands atop a plinth, and the third wall has stone elements rotated 90 degrees to create an ornamental design.

"We feel like it's time we get back to where we were a couple of hundred years ago," Arkitekt Martin Hopland founder Martin Hopland told Dezeen.

"This has the huge potential to solve three things at once," added Studio Wideroe founder Magnus Widerøe. "Reducing the waste the stone quarry produces, replacing high-intensity processed materials like concrete, and using a material that actually lasts."

Materiet Former by Ask Holmen

Norwegian architect Ask Holmen created four sculptural benches placed around the exterior of Sofienberg Church, reusing stone sourced from a local stone mason.

Holmen stacked circular, curved and rectangular slabs to form the seating, which he hopes will become places of conversation during the triennale.

"The bench is like a sunken portal – when you sit down, you are in between worlds," he told Dezeen. "It's an invitation for dialogue, and when you enter into a dialogue with someone, you never leave the same as you came in."

"I didn't know what stone elements I would get, so the elements themselves led me to the aesthetics," Holmen continued. "It's an open process and an interesting way that we can also approach architecture; maybe we can have a way of thinking that balances between rigidity and flexibility."

Open Sauna Experimental Construction by Oslo Badstuforening, Oslo School of Architecture and Design and UCLouvain-Loci

Non-profit sauna association Oslo Badstuforening worked with students and professors at the Oslo School of Architecture and Design (AHO) and Belgium's UCLouvain-Loci to build a sauna next to the Sofienberg Church.

Over two five-day sessions, master's students built the sauna from recycled building materials, including timber structure and cladding, small glass brick windows and colourful polycarbonate panels lining the split roof.

"The light coming from the top is inspired by the stained glass windows in the church," said AHO assistant professor Matthew Dylan Anderson.

"Through interviews with the target group of kids who will be using the sauna, we found out they didn't like the idea of people seeing into the sauna so that they can play with their mates, hence the small glass brick windows."

Initiating Common Ground by Studio Dreist

In the lead-up to the triennale, Vienna-based collective Studio Dreist hosted workshops where participants learned to work with cocciopesto, an ancient Roman building technique that uses lime and crushed brick.

The outcome of the workshops was a collection of air-dried panels, which were laid on a reused-timber frame to form a large communal table at the triennale exhibition.

"We were asked to make a table for the church, so we looked for materials that were local," said Studio Dreist cofounder Sophie Coqui. "Oslo has a long brick history, similar to Vienna, so we thought about how to repurpose brick into a table."

"We are curious in materials, we are not super specialised in one," added fellow cofounder Luisa Zwetkow. "We are trying to figure out how materials and processes work – it's different planning to use a material if you've already worked with it."

Oslo Architecture Triennale takes place from 17 September to 1 October at Sofienberg Church in Oslo, Norway. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
British designer duo Isabel Gibson and Helen Chesner have filled The Conran Shop's gallery with colourful, kinetic models for their London Design Festival exhibition, Motion Sickness.

Spinning orbs, flapping wings and wheeled devices all feature in the exhibition, which marks 10 years since the founding of their London-based art and design studio, Isabel + Helen.

Many of the models are prototypes, created for collaborations with brands such as Hermès and Burberry, or for installations at venues ranging from the V&A museum to the Coachella festival.

The duo wanted to give insight into the creative process behind their projects, which typically centres around model-making.

"We saw it as an opportunity to showcase the behind-the-scenes of what we do and what we make," explained Gibson, as she and Chesner gave Dezeen a tour of the show.

"The way we work, we usually jump to prototypes quite quickly," she said. "Because you can imagine how something will move and you can sketch it, but you need to get hands-on to see how it works in real life."

Movement has been a recurring theme in Isabel + Helen's work since they founded the studio in 2015, three years after graduating from Chelsea College of Arts, which is where they met.

"We've had this obsession with movement and kinetic sculpture," Gibson told Dezeen.

Read:

Is London having a design renaissance?

"Usually the movement has some form of transformation, or a reveal moment; that's something we're always interested in," added Chesner.

"The way things move also affects how you see them," she continued. "You can have so many different emotions too; something can feel really joyful or quite sinister."

The backdrop to Motion Sickness is a series of limited-edition paintings, each depicting a colourful wheel.

The designers produced these artworks with movement, using a kinetic machine they built themselves. It allows them to spin a paintbrush, forming a motif of concentric circles.

Other focal points in the show include a toy train carrying half a dozen eggs, which wobble in time with one another as the device is wheeled along the table, and a series of 15 paper spheres that spin when you pull a string.

Chesner said these projects develop through "trying stuff out and not being too precious about anything".

"A lot of the time stuff doesn't work, but you have to just constantly build on it," she said.

The exhibition also marks a decade of on-and-off collaboration between Isabel + Helen and The Conran Shop. One of the duo's first commissions was the store's LDF exhibition, A Load Of Jargon, presented in 2016 in collaboration with design website It's Nice That.

"They saw us at the beginning, when we started out, so marking 10 years with them was really nice," added Chesner.

It is among the first exhibitions that The Conran Shop has staged in the basement gallery of its store on London's Sloane Square, which has been the flagship since the closure of its previous locations on Fulham Road and Marylebone High Street.

It comes a time of reinvention for the retailer, which was founded by Sir Terence Conran in 1973. Since 2023, it has shifted its business model to focus more on its own collections rather than selling pieces by other brands.

Other recent milestones include the launch of a furniture collection with Francis Sultana, which was unveiled during last year's LDF.

Motion Sickness was on show at The Conran Shop from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Car brand Bugatti has revealed plans for a 60-storey skyscraper on the Miami River, which will be designed by US architecture studio Brandon Haw Architecture with interiors by Yabu Pushelberg.

Named Bugatti Residences Miami, the development will be the car brand's first branded residence in the US. It follows plans for its first residential skyscraper, set to be built in Dubai, which were revealed in 2023.

The tower will be the latest car-branded skyscraper to be built in the city, joining developments by luxury car brands Porsche, Bentley, Mercedes-Benz and Aston Martin.

Designed by Brandon Haw Architecture, the 60-storey skyscraper directly on the Miami River is being developed by Prosper Group and Versluys Group.

Renderings of the building, released today, show a tower split into four distinct blocks, with double-height spaces between.

The interiors of the 183 apartments and four penthouses will be designed by Yabu Pushelberg.

Read:

SHoP Architects designs Mercedes-Benz' first US residential skyscraper

According to Bugatti, the design was informed by both the architecture of Miami and the form of supercars, with a nod to the brand's C line – a motif used on Bugatti cars from the 1930s.

"Miami's bold architecture, creative spirit and global appeal make it a compelling setting for our next Bugatti Residences project," said Bugatti International managing director Wiebke Ståhl.

"Our vision is to consider every aspect, from exquisite design to seamless service and operations, creating a branded residential experience unlike any other."

The skyscraper is planned for Miami's Brickell neighbourhood, which is currently undergoing a wave of development. Major developments in the area include a 54-storey skyscraper designed by Foster + Partners and a 51-storey tower by SOM, while fashion brand Dolce & Gabbana is developing a 90-storey tower in the neighbourhood.

"Bugatti Residences Miami unites one of luxury's most respected brands with a city shaping the future of high-end real estate," said Prosper Group CEO Jay Roberts

"Miami has become the global epicenter for wealth migration, institutional investment and sophisticated living, with Brickell embodying the prime, waterfront site that is central to Prosper Group’s development strategy. It is a natural home for Bugatti’s branded residential debut in the United States."

item.content:encoded:
Cosy nooks and a study are among the spaces designed for reading at House of Shadows, a multi-generational home in Bengaluru, Karnataka, by Indian studio Cadence Architects.

Located on a quiet, tree-lined road, the house was designed for a family of bookworms who moved back to India after living in the USA for over a decade.

Cadence Architects utilised a predominantly dark, shadowy material palette for the home and fronted it with slatted screens, designed to create a feeling of seclusion and privacy.

"The client, with his young family of two children, was moving back from the USA after having stayed there for 15 years," principal architect Smaran Mallesh told Dezeen.

"As a family of readers, they wanted their home to be a repository for their books and conducive to reading," he continued.

"He wanted to build this home where he could also have his parents come and live with him."

Outside, the home is distinguished by its dark material palette, including a basalt stone base and concrete walls and a roof. A slatted timber facade screens the living spaces while allowing light and air to filter in.

According to the studio, the dark materials were all chosen for their robustness and to help the home blend with "the shadows of the trees and make the home less conspicuous on the street".

Inside, the House of Shadow's spatial organisation is intended to cater for the preferences and needs of the three generations that live there. The ground level of the home has a kitchen, living and dining area for entertaining guests.

Private living spaces for the grandparents are also on this floor.

Above, the first floor is for the parents and their children, complete with a study and reading nooks.

Described by the studio as the "more secluded and introspective" level, it was intended to offer the feeling of a quiet retreat.

Read:

Multi-generational LJ House in Ahmedabad prioritises shared living

"Books and reading spaces form an important part of the interiors, encouraging the family to pause, read, and linger," the studio said.

The third level is given over to an entertainment area for the children to enjoy with their friends. The home is complete with various terraces, decks and balconies that help keep the interiors cool.

Inside, Cadence Architects contrasted the darkness of the exterior with lighter shades through a mix of natural and local materials such as wood and lime plaster.

However, darker shades were still used in more intimate spaces, such as the reading nooks, to add a feeling of cosiness.

"We wanted to make a home that is crafted locally, with local materials," said Mallesh.

"It was important to do that for a client who is moving back and seeking his roots, in a sense. However, we were not interested in the vernacular per se but wanted a modern rendition of these traditional techniques of making."

Other multigenerational Indian houses recently featured on Dezeen include LJ House in Ahmedabad, which Studio Saransh and Iksoi Studio designed with gently curving rooflines and an asymmetrical heart-shaped stairwell, and Splitscape Residence in Coimbatore, which SpaceDNA organised around a triple-height void with an oxide-coated staircase.

A mandala-shaped bamboo truss crowns this Buddhist meditation centre in Tibet, Nepal, which is perched atop a mountain near the country's capital, Kathmandu.

Designed by architecture studio Abari, the centre contains a main hall, with a three-tiered structure that houses a 15-metre-tall meditation space, alongside a dining hall and guest house.

Find out more about the Mahamudra Meditation Centre ›

Tapmi Centre, India, by The Purple Ink Studio

Local practice The Purple Ink Studio used a canopy of parasols clad in bamboo to shelter the social hub of this business school in southwest India.

Designed to challenge conventional academic buildings, the space is organised around a sunken amphitheatre and provides a communal hub for the school's 30,000 students.

Find out more about Tapmi Centre ›

Living Bridge, Indonesia, by Jonathon Mizzi

Architect Jonathan Mizzi collaborated with students to create Living Bridge, a learning centre for a school in Indonesia.

Built from more than 300 pieces of heat-bent bamboo, the building provides a flexible space for hosting events and talks, which is partially open to the elements.

Find out more about Living Bridge ›

Chicken Hero Pavilion, Indonesia, by RAD+ar

An artificial hill was used to disguise a bamboo chicken coop, which was temporarily added to a park in Jakarta, Indonesia.

Completed by Balinese architecture studio RAD+ar, the structure was built from a bamboo lattice supported by a series of bamboo and steel columns designed as a prototype for a low-impact chicken coop.

Find out more about Chicken Hero Pavilion ›

Intaaya Retreat, Indonesia, by Pablo Luna Studio

Balinese practice Pablo Luna Studio drew on seashells, fish and manta rays for the undulating bamboo roofs of this wellness retreat in Indonesia.

Situated on the edge of a cliff on the island Nusa Penida, the retreat comprises 12 guest suites alongside a yoga studio, spa, restaurant and tea room.

Find out more about Intaaya Retreat ›

The Juliet Centre, Pakistan, by Jack Rankin and Nyami Studio

A vaulted bamboo structure frames this community workshop and event space in Pakistan, completed by Northern Irish architect Jack Rankin and UK practice Nyami Studio.

Located in Pono Village, a settlement originally developed by the Heritage Foundation of Pakistan and its founder, Yasmeen Lari, The Juliet Centre serves as a pilot scheme for zero-carbon flood-resilient homes.

Find out more about The Juliet Centre ›

Anjung, Malaysia,  by Eleena Jamil

Malaysian architect Eleena Jamil used a bamboo and green-painted steel canopy to shade this house and studio space near Kuala Lumpur.

Named Anjung, the project comprises two single-storey buildings containing a four-bedroom guesthouse in one and a small workspace in the other.

Find out more about Anjung ›

item.content:encoded:
Danish design brand Fritz Hansen has teamed up with audio specialist Technics to transform its Farringdon showroom into a series of domestic listening scenes for London Design Festival.

As part of the Fritz Hansen Sound Club, the showroom has been organised into four domestic scenes where guests are invited to listen to a curated selection of vinyl records.

The installation combines Fritz Hansen's furniture and lighting products with turntables, headphones and speakers from Japanese firm Technics.

A 90th anniversary limited edition of the Kaiser Idell Luxus table lamp and Technics' SL 40CBT turntable form the centrepiece of the various settings, both reimagined in a matching burgundy hue.

In reference to the table lamp's modernist origins, the interior styling evokes the Bauhaus movement and combines 1930s furniture with pieces from Fritz Hansen's catalogue.

Fritz Hansen Sound Club originally debuted during 3 Days of Design in Copenhagen, with the aim to explore how sound informs the way users experience interior settings.

"Sound plays a direct role in how we experience space," said Fritz Hansen creative director, Els Van Hoorebeeck. "It shapes how we move, where we pause, and how we relate to furniture, light and materials."

"With Fritz Hansen Sound Club, we explore how these elements work together to define the character of a space, and how this way of thinking continues to shape our design today."

Read:

London design "an international success story" says Sadiq Khan

The Study area pairs steel-framed desks with Arne Jacobsen's Ant Chair in a cherry veneer finish, while the designer's iconic Egg Chair provides a cosy spot for relaxing in the nearby Reading Corner.

Downstairs, the Living Room provides a setting for socialising, with a turntable and speakers oriented towards the guests.

Furniture including Poul Kjærholm's PK31 sofa and PK80 daybed creates a relaxed, lounge-like feel, while a 1930s drinks trolley and PK61 coffee tables encourage conversation and interaction.

Fritz Hansen was founded in 1872 and is known for working with famous architects and designers, including Jacobsen and Kjærholm, as well as Hans J Wegner, Børge Mogensen and Verner Panton.

More recently, the brand has collaborated with contemporary talents such as Piero Lissoni, Jamie Hayon and Cecilie Manz, who created a compact and comfortable plywood chair that can be used in a variety of contexts.

A new version of Manz's Monolit chair forms part of the presentation, alongside a more compact, wall-mounted take on the Kaiser Idell lamp and an upholstered version of Japanese studio Nendo's N02 Recycle chair.

Other highlights from this year's London Design Festival include the debut show of design platform Collate Lobby and a bamboo pavilion covered in traditional Indian police shields.

Fritz Hansen Sound Club is open daily to the public until 20 September at 78 Cowcross Street as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

The photography is by Dunka Opalko.

item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian designer Victoria Yakusha has created a sculptural, almost monochromatic interior for a jewellery brand's flagship boutique in New York City.

Also from Ukraine, the brand Guzema's store in SoHo is its first US flagship and occupies a 1,100-square-foot (102-square-metre) space on Wooster Street.

Victoria Yakusha Studio used her signature minimalist style to design a space that feels calming and curated.

"My work here was closer to that of a sculptor," said founder Victoria Yakusha. "We didn't want the feeling of traditional retail. We wanted something more intimate."

The long, narrow interior is laid out with products presented in recessed niches on both sides, and inside a series of sculptural vitrines running back through the centre.

These monolithic islands are upholstered in dove-grey suede and "rounded like a river stone" to create a soft, serene statement.

The remainder of the decor is slightly lighter in colour, with mineral-toned plaster and matching storage units creating the impression of a single cohesive surface.

In the store window, a series of white hand-sculpted vessels with textured skins and bowl-like tops are used to present Guzema's jewellery in a novel way.

Read:

Victoria Yakusha opens Miami gallery with plant-covered "living island"

These pieces follow the same visual language as the Sonaih floor lamp from Yakusha's own design brand Faina, which produces furniture, lighting and decor.

"We wanted the jewelry to feel discovered, not just displayed. That's how we came to the idea of the installation," Yakusha said. "Each vessel is hand-sculpted, layer by layer. It's an artwork in itself. It becomes part of the experience, a way of revealing something precious."

At the back of the store is a semi-private consultation area for one-on-one appointments, screened from the main space by a glass-block partition.

Several more Faina designs feature in this salon, including a curved sofa, ottoman and sconce, along with a burnished-metal table and silver tableware by Natalia Criado.

A former fashion editor, Yakusha has opened galleries for her furniture line in both Antwerp and Miami, and earlier designed the interior for Kyiv eatery Istetyka that balances rough and smooth surfaces.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, she has designed a furniture collection as an homage to her homeland and proposed a museum to preserve threatened Ukrainian cultural heritage.

The photography is by Matthew Williams.

item.content:encoded:
A green-concrete frontage marks the transformation of a neglected building in Hastings into Eagle House community centre, designed by London architecture studio IF_DO.

Eagle House was completed for community-led developer Hastings Commons and provides a mixture of public space, work areas and youth facilities.

Rather than demolish and replace the neglected Victorian building, IF_DO looked to turn it back into an active "part of the street", onto which a ground floor common room can open via large, openable windows framed by a green-concrete frontage.

"What we were really designing was civic infrastructure, a building that could hold a free community room, affordable workspace and dedicated youth facilities all at once, and do so in a way that felt genuinely welcoming rather than institutional," IF_DO co-founder Sarah Castle told Dezeen.

"Large operable windows set within deep recesses mean that people inside the common room can quite literally sit at the window and have a conversation with someone waiting for the bus outside," she added.

"The building stops being a container and becomes part of the street. In a town where many people, particularly young people, can feel invisible, that matters."

The common room of Eagle House is spread across its ground and lower ground floors. The upper area is framed in bright canary-yellow steelwork and features sit-in timber window boxes overlooking the street.

Above, three storeys of flexible, affordable work areas and counselling spaces for young people are organised around a new circulation core. This contains a lift and a repositioned, skylit staircase, also painted canary yellow.

Read:

Thing converts historic Cornish library into The Ladder arts space

The bold colour palette – chosen through sessions with members of Hastings Commons' youth organisation – continues through the building as a wayfinding strategy, with pink doorframes and walls in shades of orange, blue and green.

These colourful painted surfaces sit alongside exposed services and ducting, wood-wool wall panels and sisal flooring, keeping the spaces deliberately simple and easy to maintain while also providing acoustic comfort.

In the attic, the ceiling has been clad in timber reclaimed from the building's external walls, which have been re-rendered in pale lime, with subtly textured finishes around the windows and parapet.

"It was important that those uses were not just stacked on top of each other but genuinely connected, spatially and socially. The building needed to feel like one thing, not a collection of separate tenants," Castle said.

"We wanted the materials to feel honest and durable, things that would age well and that the community could understand and own," she added.

Elsewhere in the UK, architecture studio Thing recently converted a historic library and college in Cornwall into a community arts and culture hub, contrasting exposed, worn surfaces with new additions in timber.

Architecture collective Assemble recently converted a pair of former dairy warehouses into a community centre and church in east London.

The photography is by Killian O'Sullivan.

item.content:encoded:
Our latest roundup collects houses topped with verdant green roofs, with some designed to blend into the natural landscape and others providing elevated garden space for families to gather.

A green roof is a roof covered in vegetation that grows over a waterproof membrane and is designed to help absorb rainwater, improve insulation in the building and add wildlife to the site.

The examples below show how green roofs can be added to homes in clever ways, disguising them in their surroundings and giving residents a connection to the outdoors.

Earth, Japan, by Sou Fujimoto

Designed by Japanese architect Sou Fujimoto for hotelier Not A Hotel, this curved holiday home blends into the landscape with a garden space that rises over the rooftop from ground level.

Situated on Ishigaki Island, Japan, an oval-shaped terrace cuts into the sloping garden and leads to a living and dining room, which open onto an infinity pool and curved terrace on the other side.

Find out more about Earth ›

Forest House, Argentina, by Gonzalo Bardach Arquitectura

A ramping green roof rises over Forest House, a concrete woodland house near the coast outside Buenos Aires that was designed by local studio Gonzalo Bardach Arquitectura.

Gonzalo Bardach Arquitectura nestled the residence into a dune, creating a connection between indoor and outdoor spaces with framed views that cut through the uneven topography.

Find out more about Forest House ›

Split Mass Residence, Indonesia, by K-Thengono Design Studio

In Tangerang, Indonesia, local firm K-Thengono Design Studio created a three-storey home with sloping green roofs connecting indoor living spaces with the outdoors.

Wrapped in PE rattan facades, the house has a grassy outdoor staircase that leads residents from an open-plan kitchen, living and dining room to the swimming pool and barbecue area above.

Find out more about Split Mass Residence ›

The Inside Home, Iran, by Olgoo

The Inside Home is a subterranean holiday home in the village of Ammameh near Tehran, which Iranian architecture studio Olgoo designed in response to rapid development and loss of green spaces in the area.

Pentagonal in plan, the home is made up of three concrete blocks arranged around a central courtyard, with planting populating the roof overhead.

Find out more about The Inside Home ›

Ashraya, UK, by Kirkland Fraser Moor

A curving green roof supported by a cross-laminated timber arch soars over Ashraya, a home located in the Chiltern Hills Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty in Hertfordshire.

Bookended by two semicircular sunken courtyards, UK studio Kirkland Fraser Moor designed the two-storey house to be a contemporary addition to the landscape while also blending into the natural scenery.

Find out more about Ashraya ›

Villa Aa, Norway, by CF Møller Architects

Danish studio CF Møller Architects nestled this concrete villa into a shallow hill on a Norwegian farm, hiding it from view as people approach by disguising it under the low green roof.

Two sweeping ramps cut into the green roof to form entrances on either side of the home, skylights dot the roof to illuminate the interior and outdoor terraces overlook the nearby Oslofjord.

Find out more about Villa Aa ›

Landaburu Borda, Spain, by Jordi Hidalgo Tané

A glass corridor connects a small stone building to a subterranean green-roofed annex designed by architecture studio Jordi Hidalgo Tané.

Located in rural Navarra, Spain, Jordi Hidalgo Tané hid the concrete extension under the adjacent hillside, aiming to not disrupt the picturesque natural setting.

Find out more about Landaburu Borda ›

Forest House, Thailand, by Shma Company

Aiming to squeeze in as much greenery as possible, landscape architecture practice Shma Company planted 20 species of flora in 300 square metres of space at Forest House in Bangkok.

Accommodating seven people and 120 trees, the house is made up of three white volumes that were arranged to form two courtyards and multiple green roofs.

Find out more about Forest House ›

This week on Dezeen, we looked at the highlights of this week's London Design Festival, which included a pavilion topped with police shields.

Built on The Strand, in central London, The Pangolin Shield pavilion (pictured) has a bamboo structure topped with two types of shield – traditional Indian police shields constructed out of lathis and woven rain shields called knups.

To coincide with London Design Festival (LDF) we created an issue of Dezeen Dispatch, which was distributed at sites across the city and is available to read online here.

Highlights of LDF included the One Tool Stool exhibition by students from the Royal College of Art and a fictional 1930s hotel suite created as the backdrop for the first editions collection by new design platform Lobby.

In a Q&A with Sadiq Khan in Dezeen Dispatch, the mayor of London described the city's design as "an international success story".

Following last week's launch of Dyson's first toothbrush, we looked back at four products that the brand successfully revolutionised, and four it didn't.

Successes include vacuums, fans, hand driers and hair care products.

In architecture news, Hotelier Not A Hotel unveiled its latest unusual guesthouse – a human-sized Pokémon Poké Ball.

Set to be nestled beside a lake in Hokkaido, Japan, the three-metre-diameter spherical guest room swill be shaped like the balls used to catch creatures in the popular Pokémon game.

Reporting from Helsinki Design Week we looked at the story behind a Matti Suuronen Futuro House that has been manufactured for the first time in decades.

The creation of the house, which was on display at the festival, began when architect Jan van Dijs was made aware of an unusual post on Facebook by a friend and client.

Popular projects this week included the Pine House holiday home in southern Sweden by Johan Sundberg Arkitektur, a wooden cabin "devoted entirely to the ritual of bathing" in the UK and a "strong yet subtle" cottage extension in Scotland.

Listen to our journalists talk about the key design and architecture stories of the past seven days on our Dezeen Weekly podcast, which this week focused on London Design Festival.

The stuffed toy, called Bezzy, is part of a larger satirical campaign that draws attention to the impact of data centres and AI

item.content:encoded:
New York creative agency Basura and musician Big Data have collaborated on a stuffed toy that resembles a data centre and emits a recording from a data centre in Virginia when squeezed.

The stuffed toy, called Bezzy, is part of a larger satirical campaign that draws attention to the impact of data centres and AI as part of the launch of Big Data's first album in over seven years.

Basura founder Rajeev Basu said the team interviewed "dozens" of people living near data centres for the project and eventually shaped it into the Adopt a Data Centre campaign that includes a website, stickers, posters and Bezzy.

Overall, it imagines "AI data centers as rescue animals looking for their forever homes" according to Basura, informed by initiatives such as WWF's Adopt-a-Panda.

Basu said the toy and campaign were meant to show the absurdity of the data centre building boom, driven by AI, which has led to noise complaints from communities near the functioning data centres.

"Adopt A Data Center is an absurd and provocative invitation to look more closely at what we're being asked to welcome into our lives," Basu told Dezeen. 

Read:

First images of Gensler-designed 60-building data centre development in Utah revealed

The toy is handmade, with a soft body that depicts a data centre, a smile, eyes, and long legs and arms.

When it's squeezed, it emits a recording taken by one of the team's interviewees, a woman who lives by a data centre in Virginia.

"Hug me for ear piercing forever hum," reads a tag on Bezzy.

Basu said the interviews were prompted by the desire to understand what living near a data centre "actually feels like".

"The experiences varied, but the same concerns kept coming up: noise, light, changes to the land use and implications for local residents, and demands on local water and electricity," he said.

There are a total of 20 Bezzy toys as part of the release of Big Data's EP 4.0.

The team said the project is "not anti-AI, or anti-technology" but rather seeks to prompt questions about how AI is used responsibly.

"When the promises are so enormous, from transforming everyday life to shaping the future of humanity, the commitment to safety and accountability needs to be just as substantial," said Basu.

Massive data centres are currently being built around the world to support AI models and use large amounts of energy and water on top of the massive land usage. A recently announced hyperscale data centre for AI in Utah will have as much as 10,000 acres dedicated to the facilities.

Recently, residents from around Memphis, Tennessee, sued businessman Elon Musk over the noise pollution, reported NPR.

And beyond sound, scientists have released preliminary studies that point to a pronounced heat island effect as a result of data centre development.

The images are courtesy Basura
